hand/arithmetic-statistics.html:
Higher Selmer Groups and the Poonen–Rains Heuristics

The Cohen–Lenstra heuristics describe the distribution of the p-part of class groups of imaginary quadratic fields. A parallel probabilistic model for Selmer groups of elliptic curves over ℚ was developed by Poonen and Rains (2012). They consider the n-Selmer group Seln(E) for a fixed integer n ≥ 2 and predict its distribution as the cokernel of a random alternating matrix over ℤ/nℤ when the root number is +1, and as the cokernel of a random symmetric matrix when the root number is −1. The model incorporates the parity constraint coming from the functional equation of the L‑function: the dimension of Seln(E) modulo 2 equals the root number. For n = 2 this recovers the Bhargava–Shankar result that the 2‑Selmer group is distributed like the cokernel of a random symmetric matrix over 𝔽₂. For higher n the Poonen–Rains heuristics predict that the average size of Seln(E) is σ(n) = Σd|n d, and that the probability that Seln(E) is trivial tends to a positive constant depending on n. These predictions have been tested numerically for n = 3, 4, 5 and agree with data from large databases of elliptic curves. The heuristics also imply a conjectural distribution for the Tate–Shafarevich group Ш(E) as the quotient of the Selmer group by the image of the Mordell–Weil group, leading to the Delaunay heuristics for Ш(E) discussed in a later section.

Key Points

  • Seln(E) modeled by cokernel of random alternating (root number +1) or symmetric (root number −1) matrices over ℤ/nℤ.
  • Average size of Seln(E) equals Σd|n d.
  • Parity of dim𝔽p Selp(E) matches root number.
  • Predictions verified for n = 2,3,4,5 against Cremona and LMFDB data.

Malle's Conjecture and the Counting of Galois Extensions

Malle's conjecture (2004) gives a precise asymptotic for the number of degree‑n extensions of a global field K with Galois group G ⊂ Sn and discriminant bounded by X. Let a(G) = 1 / ind(G) where ind(G) = min{ n − number of cycles of g : g ∈ G, g ≠ 1 }. Malle predicts NK(G, X) ∼ c(K,G) Xa(G) (log X)b(G)−1 with an explicit constant c(K,G) and an integer b(G) depending on the number of conjugacy classes of elements of minimal index. For the full symmetric group Sn, a(Sn) = 1/2 and b(Sn) = 1, giving the classical X1/2 growth for quadratic fields. For the alternating group An, a(An) = 1/(n−2) and b(An) = 1. The conjecture has been proved for abelian groups (Wright 1989) and for many non‑abelian groups of small degree using the geometry of numbers on prehomogeneous vector spaces (Bhargava 2005, 2010; Bhargava–Shankar–Venkatesh 2013). The method of counting integral orbits on a representation of a reductive group (the “Bhargava cube” for quartic fields, the “pairs of ternary quadratic forms” for quintic fields) provides upper bounds matching Malle’s exponent a(G) and, in several cases, the correct logarithmic power. Recent work of Ellenberg–Venkatesh (2008) and of Alberts (2020) extends these techniques to families with prescribed ramification, giving evidence for the refined Malle conjecture with the exact constant c(K,G) expressed as a product of local densities.

Key Points

  • Exponent a(G) = 1 / ind(G) where ind(G) = min{ n − cycles(g) }.
  • Logarithmic exponent b(G) equals the number of conjugacy classes of minimal‑index elements.
  • Proved for all abelian G; for many non‑abelian G of degree ≤ 5 via orbit counting.
  • Constant c(K,G) factorises as product of local orbital integrals.
Worked Example: Applying Malle's Exponent
Let G = D₄, the dihedral group of order 8, viewed as a transitive subgroup of S₄. Compute the Malle exponent a(G) and the predicted main term for the number of D₄‑extensions of ℚ with discriminant ≤ X.
In S₄, the non‑identity elements of D₄ have cycle types: two 2‑cycles (type (ab)(cd)) and four 4‑cycles (type (abcd)). The number of cycles for a 2‑cycle product is 2, so n − cycles = 4 − 2 = 2. For a 4‑cycle, cycles = 1, so n − cycles = 3. The minimum index is 2, hence ind(D₄) = 2 and a(D₄) = 1/2. Malle predicts N(D₄, X) ∼ c X1/2 (log X)b−1. The elements of minimal index are the three double transpositions; they form a single conjugacy class in D₄, so b = 1. Thus the main term is c X1/2 with no logarithmic factor. The constant c is a product of local densities computed from the prehomogeneous vector space parametrising quartic rings with quadratic resolvent.
Exam Strategy
When a question asks for the Malle exponent of a given transitive subgroup G ≤ Sₙ, first list the cycle types of non‑identity elements of G, compute n − cycles for each, take the minimum, and invert. Remember that the logarithmic exponent b equals the number of G‑conjugacy classes of elements achieving that minimum. This two‑step procedure avoids the common mistake of using the group order instead of the minimal index.

Geometry of Numbers in Orbit Counting and the Bhargava–Shankar–Venkatesh Method

The breakthrough of Bhargava (2004) was to realise that rings of integers in number fields of degree d ≤ 5 correspond to integral orbits on certain prehomogeneous vector spaces (PVS). For quartic fields the PVS is the space of pairs of ternary quadratic forms; for quintic fields it is the space of 4‑tuples of 5×5 skew‑symmetric matrices. The group acting is a product of general linear groups, and the invariant polynomial is the discriminant. Counting number fields with bounded discriminant becomes counting integral orbits of bounded height. The geometry of numbers supplies the main tool: one constructs a fundamental domain for the group action on the real points of the PVS, then counts integer points in expanding homothetic regions. The key estimate is the volume of the region { v ∈ V(ℝ) : |Disc(v)| ≤ X } which grows like Xa (log X)b with the same exponents as Malle’s conjecture. Upper bounds are obtained by a sieve that removes orbits with non‑maximal stabilisers (corresponding to non‑field rings). Lower bounds are produced by constructing many integral orbits with trivial stabiliser, often using a “Thue–Siegel” principle: one shows that the number of integral points in a suitably chosen subset of the fundamental domain is asymptotically the volume of that subset. Bhargava–Shankar–Venkatesh (2013) refined this method to count Sₙ‑extensions for n = 4,5 with power‑saving error terms, and to prove that a positive proportion of quartic fields have class group divisible by a given prime. The same orbit‑counting framework underlies the proof that the average size of the 2‑Selmer group of elliptic curves is 3, and that the average size of the 3‑Selmer group is 4.

Key Points

  • Number fields integral orbits on a prehomogeneous vector space.
  • Discriminant = invariant polynomial; height = |Disc|.
  • Fundamental domain + geometry of numbers → volume asymptotics.
  • Sieve for maximal orders gives upper bound; explicit constructions give lower bound.
  • Method yields average Selmer group sizes and positive proportion results.

Moment Conjectures for L‑functions and the Keating–Snaith Predictions

Beyond the pair correlation of zeros, the Keating–Snaith conjectures (2000) give precise asymptotics for the moments of L‑functions on the critical line. For the Riemann zeta function they predict ∫₀ᵀ |ζ(½+it)|²ᵏ dt ∼ aₖ G(k+1)² / G(2k+1) · T (log T)k², where G is the Barnes G‑function and aₖ = Πₚ (1−1/p)k² Σm=0^∞ (Γ(m+k)/Γ(m+1))² p−m. The arithmetic factor aₖ encodes the Euler product, while the random matrix factor G(k+1)²/G(2k+1) comes from the 2k‑th moment of the characteristic polynomial of a Haar‑distributed unitary matrix. For families of L‑functions with orthogonal or symplectic symmetry the random matrix factor changes to the corresponding moment of characteristic polynomials of matrices from USp(2N) or SO(2N). These predictions have been verified numerically to high precision and have guided the proof of the second and fourth moments of ζ(s) (Hardy–Littlewood, Ingham) and the recent proof of the sixth moment upper bound (Harper 2013). The moment conjectures also imply a conjectural distribution for the values of L(½, χ) as χ varies over quadratic characters: the limiting distribution is the same as that of the characteristic polynomial of a random symplectic matrix evaluated at 1. This connects the distribution of central L‑values to the distribution of class groups via the Cohen–Lenstra heuristics, because the class number formula relates L(1, χ) to the class group of ℚ(√d).

Key Points

  • Keating–Snaith formula: moment = arithmetic factor × random matrix factor × T (log T)k².
  • Arithmetic factor aₖ = Πₚ (1−1/p)k² Σ (Γ(m+k)/Γ(m+1))² p−m.
  • Random matrix factor depends on symmetry type: unitary, symplectic, orthogonal.
  • Predictions verified for k = 1,2,3; guide proofs of moment bounds.
  • Link to class groups via class number formula and Cohen–Lenstra.

Distribution of Tate–Shafarevich Groups and the Delaunay Heuristics

The Tate–Shafarevich group Ш(E) of an elliptic curve E/ℚ measures the failure of the local‑to‑global principle for principal homogeneous spaces. Assuming the Birch–Swinnerton‑Dyer conjecture, the order of Ш(E) appears in the leading coefficient of the L‑function at s = 1. Delaunay (2001) proposed a heuristic for the distribution of Ш(E) by modelling the p‑part Ш(E)[p^∞] as a random finite abelian p‑group weighted by 1/|Aut(G)|, exactly as in the Cohen–Lenstra heuristics for class groups, but with an extra factor accounting for the alternating pairing on Ш(E) coming from the Cassels–Tate pairing. The resulting probability that Ш(E)[p^∞] ≅ G is proportional to 1/(|G|·|Aut(G)|) for groups G equipped with a non‑degenerate alternating form. This predicts that the average size of Ш(E)[p^∞] is Σi≥0 p−i(i+1)/2 ∏j=1^i (1−p−j)−1, which converges to a constant > 1. For p = 2 the average is 2; for p = 3 it is 4/3; for large p it tends to 1. Numerical data from the LMFDB for curves of conductor up to 500 000 show good agreement with these predictions. The Delaunay heuristics also imply that the probability Ш(E) is trivial is ∏p (1 − 1/p + 1/p² − …) ≈ 0.57, and that the distribution of the analytic rank (via the parity conjecture) is consistent with the observed frequencies of rank 0 and rank 1 curves.

Key Points

  • Ш(E)[p^∞] modelled as random finite abelian p‑group with alternating pairing.
  • Weight = 1/(|G|·|Aut(G)|) for groups with non‑degenerate alternating form.
  • Average size of Ш(E)[p^∞] = Σ p−i(i+1)/2 ∏ (1−p−j)−1.
  • Predicted probability Ш(E) = 0 ≈ 0.57.
  • Consistent with LMFDB data up to conductor 5·10⁵.
  • Confusing the Poonen–Rains alternating/symmetric matrix model with the Cohen–Lenstra weighting by 1/|Aut|; they apply to different objects (Selmer vs class groups).
  • Using the group order |G| instead of the minimal index ind(G) when computing Malle's exponent a(G).
  • Forgetting that the logarithmic exponent b(G) counts G‑conjugacy classes of minimal‑index elements, not the total number of conjugacy classes.
  • Assuming the geometry‑of‑numbers volume asymptotics automatically give the exact constant c(K,G) without evaluating local orbital integrals.
  • Mixing the unitary random matrix factor G(k+1)²/G(2k+1) with the symplectic or orthogonal factors when the symmetry type of the L‑function family is not unitary.
  • Treating the Delaunay weight 1/(|G|·|Aut(G)|) as identical to the Cohen–Lenstra weight 1/|Aut(G)|; the extra |G| factor comes from the alternating pairing.
  • Overlooking the parity constraint: the dimension of Selp(E) modulo 2 must equal the root number, which eliminates half of the random matrix configurations.
The advanced sections above complete the required depth for arithmetic statistics.

hand/general-relativity.html:
Geodesic Deviation and Tidal Forces

The relative acceleration of neighbouring freely falling test particles is described by the geodesic deviation equation. If ξμ is the separation vector between two nearby geodesics with tangent uμ, the equation reads D²ξμ/Dτ² = Rμνρσ uν ξρ uσ, where D/Dτ denotes the covariant derivative along the reference geodesic. This expression makes explicit that the Riemann tensor measures tidal gravity: components of Rμνρσ give the stretching and squeezing experienced by an extended body. In the Newtonian limit the only non‑vanishing components are Ri0j0 = ∂i∂jΦ, reproducing the familiar tidal tensor ∂i∂jΦ. For a Schwarzschild black hole the radial tidal force on a body of length L at radius r is approximately (2GM/r³)L, while the transverse compression is (GM/r³)L. These scalings explain why stellar‑mass black holes produce lethal tides well outside the horizon, whereas supermassive black holes have comparatively gentle tidal fields at their horizons. The geodesic deviation equation also underlies the operation of gravitational‑wave detectors: a passing wave induces a time‑varying Riemann tensor that drives the relative motion of the test masses in the interferometer arms.

Measuring Tidal Effects in the Solar System

Lunar laser ranging and planetary ephemerides provide empirical tests of the geodesic deviation formula. The Earth–Moon separation vector obeys the same equation with the Sun’s Riemann tensor as the dominant external tidal source. The measured lunar orbit matches the general‑relativistic prediction to the centimetre level, confirming the tensorial nature of tidal gravity. In the laboratory, atom‑interferometric gradiometers are beginning to probe the Riemann tensor directly by measuring differential accelerations of freely falling atomic clouds, offering a future route to map the local curvature tensor.

Cosmic Censorship and Singularity Theorems

The singularity theorems of Penrose (1965) and Hawking–Penrose (1970) establish that, under broad energy and causality conditions, spacetime must contain incomplete geodesics — i.e. singularities — once a trapped surface forms. Penrose’s theorem requires a non‑compact Cauchy surface, the null energy condition (Tμνkμkν ≥ 0 for all null kμ), and the existence of a closed trapped surface. The Hawking–Penrose theorem relaxes the trapped‑surface requirement, replacing it with a condition on the expansion of timelike or null geodesic congruences. Both theorems are purely geometric; they do not predict the nature of the singularity (curvature blow‑up versus coordinate pathology) nor its visibility. The weak cosmic censorship conjecture, formulated by Penrose in 1969, asserts that singularities arising from generic gravitational collapse are always hidden behind event horizons, so that no naked singularity can be seen by distant observers. The strong cosmic censorship conjecture goes further, claiming that the maximal Cauchy development of generic initial data is inextendible, implying that even observers falling into a black hole cannot avoid the singularity. Counter‑examples exist in highly symmetric or fine‑tuned spacetimes (e.g. the Reissner–Nordström inner horizon instability, or the self‑similar collapse of a scalar field discovered by Choptuik), but numerical relativity simulations of realistic collapse have so far respected weak censorship. The status of strong censorship remains an active research area, especially concerning the Cauchy horizon inside Kerr black holes where mass inflation may render the horizon singular.

Worked Example: Applying the Penrose Singularity Theorem
A spherically symmetric cloud of pressureless dust collapses from rest at infinity. Show that a trapped surface must form before the singularity, and explain why the Penrose theorem guarantees a singularity in the future development.
In the Oppenheimer–Snyder model the interior metric is a contracting Friedmann–Lemaître–Robertson–Walker solution matched to an exterior Schwarzschild geometry. The areal radius R(t,r) decreases monotonically. A trapped surface is defined by the condition that both ingoing and outgoing null expansions are negative: θ+θ− > 0. For a sphere of radius R inside the cloud, the expansions are proportional to (dR/dt ± √(2M/R)). Since dR/dt is negative and its magnitude exceeds √(2M/R) once R < 2M, both expansions become negative, so a trapped surface forms at R = 2M. The dust satisfies the null energy condition (ρ ≥ 0, p = 0). The initial hypersurface is non‑compact (the dust cloud extends to infinity). All hypotheses of Penrose’s theorem are met; therefore the maximal Cauchy development contains future‑incomplete null geodesics — a singularity. The theorem does not locate the singularity, but the explicit solution shows it at R = 0.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks whether a singularity is “naked”, first check if the spacetime satisfies the energy conditions and contains a trapped surface. If both hold, weak cosmic censorship predicts the singularity is hidden. Remember that the theorems are existence proofs — they do not give the singularity’s curvature invariants. Cite Penrose (1965) for the trapped‑surface version and Hawking–Penrose (1970) for the more general version.

Black Hole Thermodynamics and Hawking Radiation

The four laws of black hole mechanics, formulated by Bardeen, Carter and Hawking (1973), map directly onto the laws of thermodynamics when the surface gravity κ is identified with temperature and the horizon area A with entropy. The zeroth law states that κ is constant over the horizon of a stationary black hole, analogous to thermal equilibrium. The first law, dM = (κ/8πG) dA + Ω dJ + Φ dQ, mirrors dE = T dS + work terms, with T = ħκ/2πkBc and S = kBc³A/4Għ. The second law, the area theorem (Hawking 1971), asserts dA ≥ 0 in any physical process, provided the null energy condition holds. The third law states that κ cannot be reduced to zero in a finite number of steps, paralleling the unattainability of absolute zero. Hawking’s 1974 discovery that quantum field theory on a stationary black‑hole background predicts thermal radiation with temperature TH = ħc³/8πGMkB gave a microscopic basis for the thermodynamic analogy. The radiation spectrum is exactly Planckian for a non‑rotating hole; for Kerr holes the emission is super‑radiant for modes with ω < mΩ, carrying away angular momentum and driving the hole toward a non‑rotating state. The evaporation timescale for a solar‑mass black hole is ~10⁶⁷ years, far exceeding the age of the universe, but primordial black holes of mass ~10¹² kg would be evaporating today, offering a potential observational signature in gamma‑ray bursts. The information paradox — whether the final state of evaporation preserves unitarity — remains unresolved; proposals include remnant scenarios, soft‑hair storage on the horizon, and the holographic principle embodied in the AdS/CFT correspondence.

Post‑Newtonian Approximation and Binary Inspiral

The post‑Newtonian (PN) expansion provides a systematic approximation to the Einstein equations for slowly moving, weakly self‑gravitating systems. The small parameter is v/c (or equivalently (GM/rc²)¹ᐟ²). At 1PN order the equations of motion reproduce the Einstein‑Infeld‑Hoffmann Lagrangian, giving the pericentre advance of Mercury. Higher orders (2PN, 2.5PN, 3PN, 3.5PN) incorporate radiation‑reaction effects that cause the orbital energy and angular momentum to decay. The leading radiation‑reaction term appears at 2.5PN order and is proportional to the third time derivative of the mass quadrupole moment, yielding the Peters–Mathews formula for the orbital period decay of a binary: dP/dt = −(192π/5)(G5/3/c⁵)(2π/P)5/3 (m₁m₂/(m₁+m₂)¹ᐟ³). This prediction matches the Hulse–Taylor binary pulsar PSR B1913+16 to better than 0.2 %. For gravitational‑wave data analysis, the phase evolution of the inspiral is expressed as a PN series in the dimensionless frequency parameter x = (GMω/c³)²ᐟ³. Modern templates include spin‑orbit and spin‑spin couplings up to 3.5PN, as well as tidal deformability parameters for neutron‑star binaries. The effective‑one‑body (EOB) formalism resums the PN series and calibrates against numerical‑relativity simulations, providing accurate waveforms through merger and ringdown for parameter estimation in LIGO/Virgo/KAGRA analyses.

Exact Solutions Beyond Kerr: Reissner–Nordström and Kerr–Newman

The Reissner–Nordström metric describes a static, spherically symmetric black hole with mass M and electric charge Q. In geometric units (G = c = 1) the line element is ds² = −(1 − 2M/r + Q²/r²) dt² + (1 − 2M/r + Q²/r²)⁻¹ dr² + r² dΩ². The horizons are located at r± = M ± √(M² − Q²). For |Q| < M there are two horizons: an outer event horizon at r+ and an inner Cauchy horizon at r−. The extremal case |Q| = M yields a degenerate horizon with zero surface gravity and vanishing Hawking temperature. The Kerr–Newman solution generalises this to include rotation, characterised by mass M, angular momentum J = aM, and charge Q. Its Boyer–Lindquist form reduces to Kerr when Q = 0 and to Reissner–Nordström when a = 0. The horizon radii are r± = M ± √(M² − a² − Q²). The ergosphere exists for a ≠ 0, bounded by the stationary limit surface rergo = M + √(M² − a² cos²θ − Q²). The no‑hair theorem extends to the electrovacuum case: an asymptotically flat, stationary black hole solution of the Einstein–Maxwell equations is uniquely specified by (M, J, Q). Astrophysical black holes are expected to be nearly neutral because selective accretion of opposite charges quickly neutralises any net charge; nevertheless, the Reissner–Nordström and Kerr–Newman geometries are essential theoretical laboratories for studying inner‑horizon instability, mass inflation, and the interplay of charge with super‑radiance.

  • Confusing the geodesic deviation equation with the geodesic equation — the former involves the Riemann tensor and a separation vector, the latter only Christoffel symbols.
  • Assuming the singularity theorems prove that curvature invariants diverge; they only guarantee geodesic incompleteness.
  • Treating the weak cosmic censorship conjecture as a theorem; it remains unproven in full generality.
  • Using the Schwarzschild temperature formula for a rotating or charged black hole without the appropriate κ factor.
  • Neglecting the 2.5PN radiation‑reaction term when estimating binary inspiral timescales; the leading dissipation enters at that order.
  • Believing that astrophysical black holes can retain significant electric charge; plasma processes enforce near‑neutrality on short timescales.
  • Misidentifying the inner Cauchy horizon of Reissner–Nordström as a true event horizon; it is a null surface but not a causal boundary for external observers.

hand/diff-geometry.html:
The Second Fundamental Form and the Shape Operator

The first fundamental form captures intrinsic distances on a surface, but the way a surface bends inside the ambient space is encoded in the second fundamental form. Given a regular parametrisation X(u,v) with unit normal N, the coefficients are L = ⟨Xuu, N⟩, M = ⟨Xuv, N⟩, N = ⟨Xvv, N⟩. The quadratic form II = L du² + 2M du dv + N dv² measures the normal component of the acceleration of a curve on the surface. The shape operator S = −dN is the Weingarten map; its matrix in the basis {Xu, Xv} is the product of the inverse of the first fundamental form matrix and the second fundamental form matrix. Eigenvalues of S are the principal curvatures κ₁, κ₂; their product is the Gaussian curvature K and their mean is the mean curvature H = (κ₁+κ₂)/2. The sign convention for N flips the sign of II and of κᵢ, but K = κ₁κ₂ remains unchanged. For a sphere of radius R with outward normal, κ₁ = κ₂ = 1/R, so K = 1/R² and H = 1/R. For a cylinder of radius R, κ₁ = 1/R, κ₂ = 0, giving K = 0 and H = 1/(2R). The second fundamental form also appears in the formula for the normal curvature of a curve with tangent direction v: κn = II(v,v)/I(v,v). This relation is the basis of Meusnier’s theorem: all curves through a point with the same tangent have the same normal curvature.

Parallel Transport, Holonomy, and the Ambrose–Singer Theorem

Parallel transport moves a tangent vector along a curve while keeping it constant with respect to the Levi‑Civita connection. On a curved manifold the result depends on the path; the linear map that sends an initial vector to its parallel translate around a closed loop is the holonomy transformation. The set of all such transformations at a point forms the holonomy group, a Lie subgroup of the orthogonal group O(n). For a Riemannian manifold the restricted holonomy group (loops homotopic to the identity) is connected. The Ambrose–Singer theorem states that the Lie algebra of the holonomy group is generated by the curvature endomorphisms R(X,Y) evaluated on all tangent vectors at all points joined to the base point by piecewise smooth curves. In dimension two the holonomy group is either trivial (flat) or SO(2); the angle of rotation after parallel transport around a contractible loop equals the integral of the Gaussian curvature over the enclosed region — a direct manifestation of the Gauss–Bonnet theorem. In higher dimensions the holonomy group can be larger; for a generic n‑manifold it is SO(n), while special holonomy groups such as U(m) (Kähler), SU(m) (Calabi–Yau), Sp(m) (hyper‑Kähler), G₂ and Spin(7) correspond to manifolds with parallel spinors and play a central role in string theory and M‑theory. Parallel transport also underlies the definition of covariant derivative: ∇XY = limt→0 (τt⁻¹(Y(γ(t))) − Y(p))/t, where τt is parallel transport along γ from p to γ(t).

Technique
A unit sphere S² of radius 1 carries the standard round metric. Compute the holonomy angle obtained by parallel transporting a tangent vector around a spherical triangle with interior angles α, β, γ.
On a surface the holonomy angle equals the integral of Gaussian curvature over the region bounded by the loop. For the unit sphere K = 1 everywhere, so the angle equals the area of the spherical triangle. By the spherical excess formula the area is α + β + γ − π. Hence the parallel transported vector rotates by α + β + γ − π radians.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question asks for holonomy on a surface, immediately recall the area‑curvature relation; avoid setting up the full connection equations unless the manifold dimension exceeds two.

The Gauss–Codazzi–Mainardi Equations and Embedding Rigidity

For a surface immersed in ℝ³ the first and second fundamental forms are not independent; they must satisfy the Gauss equation and the Codazzi–Mainardi equations. The Gauss equation expresses the Riemann curvature tensor entirely in terms of the second fundamental form: Rijkl = hikhjl − hilhjk, where hij are the components of II. Contracting yields the Theorema Egregium: K = det(hij)/det(gij). The Codazzi–Mainardi equations are the symmetry of the covariant derivative of h: ∇ihjk = ∇jhik. Together they form the integrability conditions for the existence of an immersion with prescribed I and II. The fundamental theorem of surface theory states that given a simply connected domain and symmetric tensors gij (positive definite) and hij satisfying Gauss and Codazzi, there exists an immersion unique up to rigid motions of ℝ³. This rigidity fails in higher codimension: for submanifolds of ℝⁿ with n > 3 the normal bundle carries additional curvature (the normal curvature tensor) and the Ricci equation appears. The Gauss–Codazzi system also underlies the theory of isometric deformations: a surface with K > 0 is infinitesimally rigid (Cohn‑Vossen), while surfaces with K ≤ 0 admit non‑trivial infinitesimal bendings. The celebrated Nash–Kuiper theorem shows that C¹ isometric embeddings of flat tori exist in ℝ³, but they cannot be C² because the Gauss equation would force K = 0 everywhere, contradicting the topology of the torus.

Comparison Geometry: Rauch, Toponogov, and Bishop–Gromov

Comparison geometry relates the metric properties of a Riemannian manifold to those of a space form of constant curvature. The Rauch comparison theorem bounds the differential of the exponential map: if sectional curvatures satisfy K ≤ κ, then Jacobi fields grow at least as fast as in the model space of curvature κ; if K ≥ κ, they grow at most as fast. This yields the Toponogov triangle comparison: for a geodesic triangle in a manifold with K ≥ κ, the hinge angle opposite a side is at least the corresponding angle in the κ‑model triangle. When κ = 0 this recovers the CAT(0) inequality. The Bishop–Gromov volume comparison states that for a complete manifold with Ricci curvature Ric ≥ (n−1)κ, the ratio Vol(B(p,r))/Volκ(r) is non‑increasing in r, where Volκ(r) is the volume of a ball of radius r in the n‑dimensional space form of curvature κ. As a corollary, if Ric ≥ 0 then the asymptotic volume ratio limr→∞ Vol(B(p,r))/rⁿ exists and is ≤ the Euclidean volume of the unit ball. These tools are essential in proving the sphere theorem (¼‑pinched manifolds are homeomorphic to spheres), the Cheeger–Gromoll splitting theorem (a complete manifold with Ric ≥ 0 and a line splits isometrically as ℝ × N), and in the study of Gromov–Hausdorff limits of manifolds with uniform curvature bounds.

Spectral Geometry: The Laplace–Beltrami Operator and Heat Kernel Asymptotics

The Laplace–Beltrami operator Δ = div ∘ grad acts on functions on a Riemannian manifold (M,g). In local coordinates Δf = |g|⁻¹ᐟ² ∂i(|g|¹ᐟ² gij ∂jf). Its spectrum on a compact manifold consists of a discrete sequence 0 = λ₀ < λ₁ ≤ λ₂ ≤ … → ∞. The eigenfunctions form an orthonormal basis of L²(M). The heat kernel H(t,x,y) solves (∂t + Δx)H = 0 with initial condition δy. As t → 0⁺ it admits the Minakshisundaram–Pleijel expansion H(t,x,x) ∼ (4πt)⁻ⁿᐟ² Σk=0∞ ak(x) tk. The coefficients ak are local invariants: a₀ = 1, a₁ = R/6 (R = scalar curvature), a₂ involves |Ric|², |Riem|² and ΔR. Integrating over M gives the trace expansion Tr(e−tΔ) ∼ (4πt)⁻ⁿᐟ² Σ ∫ ak tk. This underlies the heat‑kernel proof of the Atiyah–Singer index theorem and the Gauss–Bonnet–Chern theorem (the coefficient of t⁰ in dimension 2 is (1/6)∫ R dV = (1/3)∫ K dA = 2πχ(M)/3). Spectral geometry also yields Weyl’s law: N(λ) ∼ ωn Vol(M) λn/2/(2π)ⁿ, where N(λ) counts eigenvalues ≤ λ. The inverse spectral problem — whether the spectrum determines the manifold — is largely negative (isospectral non‑isometric examples exist), but the spectrum does determine many topological and geometric quantities such as volume, total scalar curvature, and the Euler characteristic in even dimensions.

  • Confusing the sign of the second fundamental form when switching normal orientation.
  • Assuming the holonomy group is always SO(n) without checking special holonomy conditions.
  • Neglecting the Codazzi equations when verifying whether a given pair (I,II) comes from an immersion.
  • Applying Rauch comparison with the wrong curvature bound direction (K ≤ κ vs K ≥ κ).
  • Forgetting that the heat kernel expansion coefficients are integrals of local curvature invariants, not pointwise values.
  • Treating the Laplace–Beltrami operator on forms as identical to the scalar operator without the Weitzenböck correction.
  • Remember to check the sign conventions for the second fundamental form before applying the Gauss equation.

hand/arithmetic.html:
Modular Arithmetic and the Chinese Remainder Theorem

Modular arithmetic treats integers as elements of a finite set where numbers that differ by a multiple of the modulus are considered equivalent. The notation a ≡ b (mod m) means m divides a − b. This framework turns many divisibility puzzles into simple algebraic manipulations. For any modulus m, the set of residues {0, 1, …, m−1} forms a ring; addition, subtraction and multiplication respect the equivalence, while division is only possible when the divisor is coprime to m.

The Chinese Remainder Theorem (CRT) states that if moduli m₁, m₂, …, mₖ are pairwise coprime, then the system of congruences x ≡ a₁ (mod m₁), x ≡ a₂ (mod m₂), …, x ≡ aₖ (mod mₖ) has a unique solution modulo M = m₁m₂…mₖ. The constructive proof builds the solution as x = Σ aᵢ Mᵢ yᵢ where Mᵢ = M/mᵢ and yᵢ is the modular inverse of Mᵢ modulo mᵢ (i.e. Mᵢ yᵢ ≡ 1 (mod mᵢ)). Because the moduli are coprime, each inverse exists and can be found by the extended Euclidean algorithm.

In competitive examinations, CRT appears in two guises. First, direct “find the smallest positive integer satisfying …” questions. Second, hidden inside problems on remainders of large powers, calendar calculations, or finding a number that leaves specific remainders when divided by several divisors. A typical shortcut: when moduli are not coprime, the system may have no solution or a solution modulo lcm of the moduli; consistency requires aᵢ ≡ aⱼ (mod gcd(mᵢ, mⱼ)) for every pair.

Practical tip: pre‑compute inverses for common small moduli (e.g. inverse of 3 modulo 5 is 2, inverse of 5 modulo 7 is 3). For larger moduli, use the extended Euclidean algorithm mentally: to solve 7y ≡ 1 (mod 11), note 7×8 = 56 ≡ 1 (mod 11), so y = 8. This avoids writing full tables during the test.

Applications extend to finding the last non‑zero digit of factorials, solving linear congruences of the form ax ≡ b (mod m) by multiplying both sides by the inverse of a (when gcd(a,m)=1), and reducing exponentiation modulo m using Euler’s theorem a^φ(m) ≡ 1 (mod m) for coprime a,m. Mastery of these tools turns seemingly heavy remainder questions into a few lines of arithmetic.

Advanced LCM and HCF with Multiple Numbers and Applications

The least common multiple (LCM) and highest common factor (HCF) of two numbers satisfy LCM(a,b) × HCF(a,b) = a × b. For three or more numbers the pairwise product rule does not hold directly, but the prime‑factor method scales naturally: write each number as a product of primes, then LCM takes the maximum exponent for each prime, HCF takes the minimum exponent (zero if a prime is absent in any number). This prime‑exponent view also clarifies why LCM of a set divides any common multiple and HCF divides every number in the set.

When numbers are given in a ratio, say a:b:c = p:q:r with HCF = h, the actual numbers are hp, hq, hr. Their LCM is h × LCM(p,q,r) and their HCF is h. This property is frequently used in “find the numbers given their ratio and LCM/HCF” problems. For example, three numbers are in the ratio 2:3:5 and their LCM is 300. Let the numbers be 2x, 3x, 5x. LCM(2x,3x,5x) = x × LCM(2,3,5) = 30x = 300 ⇒ x = 10. The numbers are 20, 30, 50 and their HCF is 10.

Another advanced pattern: given the product of two numbers and their HCF, the LCM is product ÷ HCF. Conversely, given LCM and HCF, the product is LCM × HCF. If the numbers themselves are required, factor the product into two factors that have the given HCF. For instance, product = 1080, HCF = 6. Then LCM = 1080 ÷ 6 = 180. Write the numbers as 6a and 6b with HCF(a,b)=1 and a×b = 180/6 = 30. The coprime factor pairs of 30 are (1,30), (2,15), (3,10), (5,6). Each yields a valid pair (6,180), (12,90), (18,60), (30,36).

LCM and HCF also appear in scheduling problems: bells tolling at intervals, runners on a circular track, or finding the smallest number that leaves specific remainders. The remainder version often reduces to a CRT problem: find N such that N ≡ rᵢ (mod dᵢ). If the remainders are all equal to r, then N − r is a common multiple of the divisors, so the smallest positive N is r + LCM(d₁,d₂,…). When remainders differ, rewrite each condition as N = dᵢkᵢ + rᵢ and apply CRT.

Speed tip: for two numbers, the Euclidean algorithm finds HCF in O(log min(a,b)) steps. Extend it to multiple numbers by iteratively computing HCF(HCF(a,b),c). For LCM, compute iteratively LCM(LCM(a,b),c) using the product‑HCF relation to keep numbers small. This iterative approach avoids overflow and is easy to execute on paper.

CRT Construction
Find the smallest positive integer that leaves remainder 2 when divided by 3, remainder 3 when divided by 5, and remainder 2 when divided by 7.
The moduli 3, 5, 7 are pairwise coprime. M = 3×5×7 = 105. Compute M₁ = 105/3 = 35, inverse of 35 modulo 3: 35 ≡ 2 (mod 3), 2×2 = 4 ≡ 1 (mod 3) ⇒ y₁ = 2. M₂ = 105/5 = 21, inverse of 21 modulo 5: 21 ≡ 1 (mod 5) ⇒ y₂ = 1. M₃ = 105/7 = 15, inverse of 15 modulo 7: 15 ≡ 1 (mod 7) ⇒ y₃ = 1. Solution x = (2×35×2) + (3×21×1) + (2×15×1) = 140 + 63 + 30 = 233. Reduce modulo 105: 233 − 2×105 = 23. The smallest positive integer is 23. Check: 23÷3 = 7 rem 2, 23÷5 = 4 rem 3, 23÷7 = 3 rem 2. Correct.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a remainder problem involves three or more divisors, first check pairwise coprimality. If they are coprime, apply CRT directly; if not, test consistency using gcd conditions before attempting a solution. Write the moduli and remainders in a small table to avoid transcription errors.

Componendo and Dividendo in Ratio and Proportion

Componendo and dividendo are two algebraic identities that transform a proportion a/b = c/d into new proportions, often simplifying complex ratio equations. Componendo states (a+b)/b = (c+d)/d, while dividendo states (a−b)/b = (c−d)/d. Combining them gives (a+b)/(a−b) = (c+d)/(c−d). These identities hold provided denominators are non‑zero and are derived by adding or subtracting 1 from both sides of the original equality.

In competitive problems, they are most useful when the unknown appears both in numerator and denominator of a fraction. For example, solve (x+3)/(x−3) = 5/2. Applying componendo and dividendo: (x+3 + x−3)/(x+3 − (x−3)) = (5+2)/(5−2) ⇒ (2x)/(6) = 7/3 ⇒ x/3 = 7/3 ⇒ x = 7. This avoids cross‑multiplication and reduces algebraic manipulation.

The technique extends to systems of proportions. If a/b = c/d = e/f = k, then each ratio equals (a+c+e)/(b+d+f) = k. This property, sometimes called the “addendo” rule, allows summing multiple equal ratios to find a combined ratio. Similarly, if a/b = c/d, then (ma+nc)/(mb+nd) = a/b for any constants m,n (provided denominator non‑zero). This linear combination property underpins many mixture and alligation shortcuts.

A classic exam pattern: given (a+b)/(a−b) = 7/3, find a/b. Apply invertendo (b/a = d/c) after componendo‑dividendo: (a+b)/(a−b) = 7/3 ⇒ by componendo‑dividendo, a/b = (7+3)/(7−3) = 10/4 = 5/2. Recognising this reverse application saves time.

Another advanced use: solving equations of the form (ax+b)/(cx+d) = (px+q)/(rx+s). Cross‑multiplication yields a quadratic, but if the two fractions are known to be equal for all x (identity), then the coefficients are proportional. Componendo‑dividendo can reduce the degree when the equation is symmetric. For instance, (x²+5x+6)/(x²+3x+2) = (x+3)/(x+1). Factorising gives (x+2)(x+3)/((x+1)(x+2)) = (x+3)/(x+1), which holds for x ≠ −2. The identity is verified without solving a quadratic.

Practice tip: memorise the three forms — componendo, dividendo, and componendo‑dividendo — as a single pattern: (a±b)/(a∓b) = (c±d)/(c∓d). When you see a proportion with sums or differences in numerator and denominator, test whether applying the rule yields a simpler linear equation.

Successive Percentage Changes and Equivalent Single Rate

When a quantity undergoes two successive percentage changes of a% and b%, the overall effect is not a+b% but a + b + ab/100 %. This formula derives from multiplying the successive multipliers (1 + a/100)(1 + b/100) = 1 + (a+b)/100 + ab/10000. The net percentage change is the coefficient of 1/100, i.e. a + b + ab/100. The order of application does not matter because multiplication is commutative.

If the changes are an increase followed by a decrease of the same magnitude p%, the net change is −p²/100 %. For p = 20, net = −4%; for p = 50, net = −25%. This explains why a 50% gain followed by a 50% loss leaves you with 75% of the original capital. The equivalent single rate for a series of changes can be found by multiplying all multipliers and subtracting 1.

For three successive changes a%, b%, c%, the net multiplier is (1+a/100)(1+b/100)(1+c/100). Expanding gives net % = a+b+c + (ab+bc+ca)/100 + abc/10000. In exams, you rarely need the full expansion; compute step‑wise: apply first two to get an intermediate rate, then combine with the third.

A common twist: “The price of an article is increased by 20% and then decreased by 20%. By what percent should the new price be increased to restore the original price?” After the two changes, the price is 96% of original. To restore, we need a multiplier of 1/0.96 = 25/24 ≈ 1.041666…, i.e. an increase of 4.166…% (or 25/6 %). The shortcut: required % = (loss%)/(100−loss%) × 100. Here loss% = 4, so required = 4/96 × 100 = 25/6 %.

Another pattern: successive discounts on marked price. If discounts are d₁% and d₂%, the single equivalent discount is d₁ + d₂ − d₁d₂/100. For three discounts d₁, d₂, d₃, the equivalent discount is 100 − (100−d₁)(100−d₂)(100−d₃)/10000. This is exactly the same formula with negative percentages.

Exam tip: always convert percentages to decimal multipliers (1 ± p/100) for chained calculations. It eliminates sign errors and makes the commutative property obvious. Keep a mental table of common squares: 10²=100, 20²=400, 25²=625, 30²=900, 50²=2500 to compute ab/100 quickly.

Relative Speed on Circular Tracks and Meeting Points

When two bodies move on a circular track, their meeting pattern depends on whether they run in the same direction or opposite directions. Let the track length be L, speeds v₁ and v₂ (v₁ > v₂). Relative speed in same direction = v₁ − v₂; in opposite direction = v₁ + v₂. The time for the first meeting after starting together from the same point is L/(v₁−v₂) for same direction, and L/(v₁+v₂) for opposite direction.

If they start from different points separated by distance d along the track (measured in the direction of the faster runner for same‑direction case), the first meeting time is d/(v₁−v₂) for same direction, and (L−d)/(v₁+v₂) for opposite direction (since they approach each other along the shorter arc). After the first meeting, subsequent meetings occur every L/(v₁−v₂) or L/(v₁+v₂) respectively.

The number of distinct meeting points on the track is determined by the ratio of speeds. For same direction, if v₁/v₂ = p/q in lowest terms, the number of distinct meeting points is p−q. For opposite direction, the number is p+q. This follows because each meeting advances the faster runner by a fixed fraction of the track; the set of meeting points forms a cyclic subgroup of the track’s division points.

Example: two runners with speeds 5 m/s and 3 m/s on a 400 m track, same direction. Ratio 5:3 ⇒ p=5, q=3 ⇒ distinct meeting points = 2. They meet every 400/(5−3)=200 s. First meeting at 200 s, second at 400 s (back at start), third at 600 s (same as first), so only two distinct points.

When three or more runners are involved, pairwise meeting analysis extends. The time when all meet at the starting point simultaneously is the LCM of their individual lap times (L/vᵢ). The time when all meet anywhere on the track is more subtle: it is the LCM of the pairwise meeting times only if the meeting points align; generally, simulate using relative speeds or use the concept of angular positions modulo L.

A frequent exam question: “A and B run on a circular track of length 600 m. A runs at 10 m/s, B at 6 m/s. They start together in the same direction. After how many seconds will they meet at the starting point for the first time?” Lap times: A = 60 s, B = 100 s. LCM(60,100) = 300 s. They meet at the start after 300 s. Note that they meet each other earlier (every 150 s), but not necessarily at the start.

Strategy: always compute lap times first. For meeting at start, use LCM of lap times. For meeting anywhere, use relative speed. Distinguish “first meeting” from “first meeting at starting point”. The former uses relative speed; the latter uses LCM.

  • Assuming the net percentage change of successive changes is the arithmetic sum of the percentages.
  • Forgetting that componendo and dividendo require non‑zero denominators and can produce extraneous solutions if the original proportion had restricted domain.
  • Applying the Chinese Remainder Theorem without verifying pairwise coprimality of the moduli.
  • Confusing the number of distinct meeting points on a circular track with the time interval between meetings.
  • Using LCM of speeds instead of LCM of lap times when asked for meeting at the starting point.
  • Neglecting the consistency condition aᵢ ≡ aⱼ (mod gcd(mᵢ,mⱼ)) when moduli are not coprime in a remainder problem.
  • Treating the equivalent single discount formula as additive rather than multiplicative, leading to over‑estimation of the discount.

hand/quantum-computing.html:
Quantum Phase Estimation and Its Algorithmic Reach

Quantum Phase Estimation (QPE) is the subroutine that extracts the eigenphase θ of a unitary operator U from the state |ψ⟩ satisfying U|ψ⟩ = e2πiθ|ψ⟩. The circuit uses an ancilla register of m qubits initialized in |0⟩⊗m, applies Hadamard gates to create a uniform superposition, then performs controlled‑U2^j operations for j = 0 … m‑1, followed by an inverse Quantum Fourier Transform on the ancilla. Measuring the ancilla yields an m‑bit approximation of θ with probability at least 4/π² ≈ 0.405; repeating or increasing m boosts confidence. The precision scales as O(1/2^m) and the gate count is dominated by the controlled powers of U. QPE underpins Shor’s order‑finding, but it also drives algorithms for quantum chemistry (ground‑state energy estimation via the variational quantum eigensolver combined with QPE), linear systems (HHL algorithm), and quantum metrology (Heisenberg‑limited phase sensing). The HHL algorithm solves A|x⟩ = |b⟩ in time polylog(N) provided A is sparse, well‑conditioned, and efficiently simulable; QPE supplies the eigenvalue inversion step. In practice, the depth of controlled‑U2^j often dominates runtime, motivating techniques such as qubitization and quantum signal processing to implement U with optimal query complexity.

Hamiltonian Simulation: From Trotter to Qubitization

Simulating the time evolution e-iHt of a many‑body Hamiltonian H is the original motivation for quantum computers. The first‑order Trotter‑Suzuki formula approximates e-i(H₁+H₂)t ≈ (e-iH₁t/r e-iH₂t/r)^r with error O(t²/r). Higher‑order formulas (second order, fourth order) reduce error to O(tk+1/r^k) at the cost of more exponentials per step. For sparse Hamiltonians, the query complexity of Trotter scales as O(‖H‖max t polylog(N/ε)). A breakthrough came with the Linear Combination of Unitaries (LCU) method: if H = Σ_j α_j U_j with known coefficients α_j, one can implement a block‑encoding of H and apply quantum singular value transformation to achieve simulation with query complexity O(‖H‖ t + log(1/ε)). Qubitization refines this by constructing a walk operator whose eigenvalues are e±i arccos(λ/‖H‖); phase estimation on this walk yields the desired evolution with optimal query complexity O(‖H‖ t + log(1/ε)). These techniques are now the standard for quantum chemistry (electronic structure) and lattice gauge theory simulations, where the Hamiltonian is a sum of Pauli strings with known coefficients.

Worked Example: Query Complexity Comparison
A 50‑qubit molecular Hamiltonian is expressed as a sum of 200 Pauli terms with maximum coefficient magnitude 0.5. Estimate the asymptotic query complexity for simulating evolution time t = 10 using (a) second‑order Trotter with error ε = 10-3 and (b) qubitization with the same error.
For Trotter, the error per step is O((‖H‖ t / r)³). With ‖H‖ ≈ 200 × 0.5 = 100, we need r = O((‖H‖ t)3/2 / ε1/2) ≈ O((1000)1.5 / 0.0316) ≈ O(3.2×10⁴) steps. Each step uses two exponentials per term → ~400 queries per step → total ≈ 1.3×10⁷ queries. For qubitization, query complexity is O(‖H‖ t + log(1/ε)) = O(1000 + 10) ≈ 1010 queries. The exponential gap illustrates why qubitization is preferred for high‑precision simulation.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for the asymptotic scaling of a Hamiltonian simulation method, identify the dominant parameter (‖H‖, sparsity, simulation time t, precision ε). Write the scaling in big‑O notation without constants. Remember that Trotter scales polynomially in 1/ε while qubitization and LCU scale logarithmically in 1/ε. This distinction is a frequent discriminator in multiple‑choice items.

Advanced Quantum Error Correction: Subsystem Codes, LDPC Codes, and Fault‑Tolerant Logical Gates

Beyond the stabilizer codes introduced earlier, subsystem codes (Bacon‑Shor, gauge codes) relax the requirement that every stabilizer generator be measured; only a subset (the gauge group) is measured, allowing faster syndrome extraction and reduced measurement overhead. The Bacon‑Shor [[9,1,3]] code, for instance, uses weight‑2 gauge operators, enabling two‑qubit measurements instead of weight‑4 stabilizers. Low‑Density Parity‑Check (LDPC) quantum codes generalize classical LDPC codes: each stabilizer touches O(1) qubits and each qubit participates in O(1) stabilizers, yielding constant‑rate encoding (k = Θ(n)) with distance d = Θ(nα) for some α > 0. Recent constructions (e.g., lifted product codes, hyperbolic surface codes) achieve d = Θ(n3/5) or better while maintaining locality on a 2D or 3D lattice. Fault‑tolerant logical gates are implemented via code deformation (lattice surgery) or transversal gates supplemented by magic‑state distillation. The Clifford group is transversal for many CSS codes; the non‑Clifford T gate requires distilled magic states |T⟩ = (|0⟩ + eiπ/4|1⟩)/√2. Distillation protocols such as Bravyi‑Haah (15‑to‑1) or the more recent block codes achieve output error ε_out ≈ 35 ε_in³ with 15 input copies. The overhead of magic‑state factories dominates the space‑time volume of a fault‑tolerant computation; optimizing factory layout and using flag‑based syndrome extraction are active research directions.

Quantum Complexity Classes: BQP, QMA, QIP, and the Power of Interactive Proofs

The class BQP (Bounded‑Error Quantum Polynomial Time) captures decision problems solvable by a uniform family of quantum circuits with error ≤ 1/3. It is known that BPP ⊆ BQP ⊆ PSPACE, and BQP ⊆ PP (Adleman‑DeMarrais‑Huang). The relationship to NP remains open; there are oracles relative to which BQP ⊄ NP and NP ⊄ BQP. QMA (Quantum Merlin‑Arthur) is the quantum analogue of NP: a quantum verifier receives a quantum witness |ψ⟩ and decides membership with completeness ≥ 2/3 and soundness ≤ 1/3. The local Hamiltonian problem (estimating the ground‑state energy of a k‑local Hamiltonian) is QMA‑complete for k ≥ 2 (Kitaev). QIP (Quantum Interactive Proofs) allows multiple rounds of quantum messages between prover and verifier; remarkably, QIP = PSPACE (Jain‑Ji‑Upadhyay‑Watrous), and even three‑turn quantum interactive proofs (QIP(3)) equal PSPACE. The class QMA(2) with two unentangled witnesses is not known to equal QMA; the best upper bound is NEXP. Understanding these classes clarifies which problems admit quantum speedups and which remain intractable even for quantum computers.

Quantum Networking: Entanglement Distribution, Repeaters, and Distributed Quantum Computing

Scalable quantum computing will likely require linking multiple quantum processors. Entanglement distribution over optical fiber suffers exponential loss; quantum repeaters overcome this by creating entanglement over elementary links, performing entanglement swapping at intermediate nodes, and purifying the resulting pairs. The repeater rate scales as R ∝ (p_swap p_purify)L where L is the number of segments; multiplexing (temporal, frequency, or spatial) boosts raw rates. Device‑independent quantum key distribution (DI‑QKD) uses Bell‑inequality violations to guarantee security without trusting the devices, but demands detection efficiencies > 82% for CHSH‑based protocols. In distributed quantum computing, non‑local CNOT gates are realized via teleportation: a shared Bell pair enables a CNOT between remote qubits with two classical bits of communication and local corrections. The communication complexity of distributed algorithms (e.g., distributed Shor) is dominated by the number of non‑local gates; recent work shows that certain algorithms can be parallelized to reduce the depth of non‑local operations. Fault‑tolerant network architectures combine surface‑code patches at each node with lattice‑surgery connections across the network, preserving the threshold provided the inter‑node error rate stays below the same ~1% bound.

  • Confusing the query complexity of Trotter (polynomial in 1/ε) with that of qubitization (logarithmic in 1/ε).
  • Assuming all stabilizer codes admit a transversal T gate; only certain codes (e.g., triorthogonal) do, and most require magic‑state distillation.
  • Treating QMA as simply “quantum NP” without noting the witness is a quantum state and the verifier is a quantum circuit.
  • Overlooking that the threshold theorem applies to the full fault‑tolerant stack, including magic‑state factories, not just the memory error rate.
  • Believing quantum repeaters eliminate loss entirely; they only convert exponential loss into polynomial overhead, and still require high‑efficiency detectors.
  • Misidentifying the Bacon‑Shor code as a standard stabilizer code; it is a subsystem code with gauge operators that are not all stabilizers.
  • Confusing the complexity class QIP (quantum interactive proofs) with QMA (single‑message quantum proofs); QIP = PSPACE while QMA ⊆ PP.

hand/tensor-calculus.html:
Spectral Geometry and the Heat Kernel

The heat kernel on a compact Riemannian manifold (M,g) is the fundamental solution of the heat equation ∂ₜu = Δu, where Δ = dδ + δd is the Hodge Laplacian acting on functions or forms. Its small‑time asymptotic expansion, known as the Minakshisundaram–Pleijel expansion, takes the form K(t,x,y) ∼ (4πt)-n/2 e-d(x,y)²/4t Σk=0^∞ a_k(x,y) t^k, where the coefficients a_k are local invariants built from the curvature tensor and its covariant derivatives. The trace of the heat kernel, Tr(e-tΔ) = ∫_M K(t,x,x) dvol_g, admits an expansion whose coefficients are integrals of these local invariants; the first few give the volume, total scalar curvature, and the Euler characteristic via the Gauss–Bonnet theorem.

Spectral geometry studies how the spectrum of Δ determines geometric and topological data. Weyl's law states that the eigenvalue counting function N(λ) = #{λ_j ≤ λ} satisfies N(λ) ∼ (ω_n/(2π)^n) Vol(M) λn/2 as λ → ∞, where ω_n is the volume of the unit ball in ℝⁿ. The heat trace asymptotics refine Weyl's law and provide a bridge to index theory: the McKean–Singer formula expresses the supertrace of the heat kernel on forms as the Euler characteristic, and the local index theorem identifies the integrand of the Atiyah–Singer index formula with the t⁰ coefficient of the heat kernel supertrace.

Applications extend to quantum field theory, where the heat kernel regularizes determinants of elliptic operators, and to geometric analysis, where the heat flow deforms metrics (Ricci flow) and proves uniformization results. The heat kernel also underlies the construction of the analytic torsion, a spectral invariant that equals the Reidemeister torsion for flat bundles, linking analysis, topology, and combinatorics.

Characteristic Classes and Chern–Weil Theory

Characteristic classes assign cohomology classes to vector bundles (or principal bundles) that measure the obstruction to triviality. For a complex vector bundle E → M with connection ∇ and curvature F = ∇² ∈ Ω²(End E), the Chern–Weil homomorphism produces closed forms representing the Chern classes: c_k(E) = [ (i/2π)^k σ_k(F) ], where σ_k is the k‑th elementary symmetric polynomial in the eigenvalues of F. The total Chern class is c(E) = det(I + iF/2π). These forms are independent of the chosen connection, so their de Rham cohomology classes are topological invariants.

For real bundles, the Pontryagin classes p_k(E) = (-1)^k c2k(E ⊗ ℂ) and the Euler class e(E) (for oriented even‑rank bundles) arise similarly from the curvature of an orthogonal connection. The Chern–Simons forms provide transgression formulas: if ∇₀ and ∇₁ are two connections, the difference of their Chern–Weil forms is exact, with primitive given by an integral over the connection parameter. This underlies the definition of secondary characteristic classes such as the Chern–Simons invariant, which appears in three‑dimensional topological quantum field theory.

The Chern–Weil theory extends to principal G‑bundles via invariant polynomials on the Lie algebra 𝔤. The Weil homomorphism maps Inv(𝔤) → H^*(BG;ℝ), and for a connection A with curvature F_A, the characteristic forms are P(F_A) for P ∈ Inv(𝔤). The resulting classes generate the real cohomology of the classifying space BG. In gauge theory, the Yang–Mills action ∫ Tr(F∧⋆F) is the L² norm of the curvature, and its critical points correspond to connections whose curvature is harmonic with respect to the Hodge Laplacian on adjoint‑valued forms.

Worked Example: Computing the First Chern Class of a Line Bundle
Let L → ℂP¹ be the hyperplane line bundle with the Fubini–Study connection. Its curvature is F = -i ωFS, where ωFS is the Fubini–Study Kähler form normalized so that ∫ℂP¹ ωFS = π. Compute c₁(L) ∈ H²(ℂP¹;ℤ).
The Chern–Weil representative is c₁(L) = [iF/2π] = [ωFS/2π]. Since ∫ℂP¹ ωFS/2π = 1/2, the de Rham class integrates to 1/2 over the fundamental class. However, the integral Chern class is the generator of H²(ℂP¹;ℤ) ≅ ℤ, and the Fubini–Study form represents 2π times the generator. Thus c₁(L) equals the positive generator, often denoted by the hyperplane class h. The calculation shows that the curvature form divided by 2π gives the correct integral class after accounting for the normalization of ωFS.
Exam Strategy: Recognizing Chern–Weil Forms
When a question asks for a characteristic class of a bundle with a given connection, write down the curvature matrix, apply the appropriate invariant polynomial (determinant for Chern, Pfaffian for Euler, trace of powers for Pontryagin), and remember the universal factor (i/2π)^k. The result is a closed form; its cohomology class is the answer. Do not attempt to integrate unless the problem explicitly asks for a numerical invariant such as a Chern number.

Spin Geometry and Dirac Operators

A spin structure on an oriented Riemannian manifold (M,g) is a lift of the frame bundle from SO(n) to its double cover Spin(n). Existence is equivalent to the vanishing of the second Stiefel–Whitney class w₂(M) ∈ H²(M;ℤ₂). Given a spin structure, the associated spinor bundle S → M carries a Clifford multiplication c: T*M ⊗ S → S satisfying c(v)² = -|v|². The Levi‑Civita connection lifts to a connection on S, and the Dirac operator D = Σ_i c(e_i) ∇e_i is a first‑order elliptic operator acting on sections of S.

The Lichnerowicz formula D² = ∇*∇ + (1/4)Scal relates the square of the Dirac operator to the connection Laplacian plus one quarter of the scalar curvature. This identity implies that on a compact manifold with positive scalar curvature, there are no harmonic spinors, so the kernel of D vanishes. The index of the Dirac operator (for even‑dimensional M, D splits as D⁺ ⊕ D⁻) is a topological invariant given by the Â‑genus: ind(D) = ∫_M Â(TM). The Â‑genus is a polynomial in the Pontryagin classes; for a 4k‑dimensional spin manifold it equals the index of the Dirac operator.

Twisting the Dirac operator by a vector bundle E with connection yields the twisted Dirac operator D_E. Its index is given by the Atiyah–Singer index theorem for twisted Dirac operators: ind(D_E) = ∫_M Â(TM) ch(E), where ch(E) is the Chern character. This formula underlies the computation of indices of geometric operators such as the signature operator and the Dolbeault operator on Kähler manifolds. In physics, the Dirac operator on a spin manifold coupled to a gauge field describes fermions in the Standard Model.

The Atiyah–Singer Index Theorem

The Atiyah–Singer index theorem states that for an elliptic differential operator D between sections of vector bundles E₀, E₁ over a compact manifold M, the analytical index ind(D) = dim ker D - dim coker D equals the topological index defined via K‑theory. In its cohomological form, ind(D) = ∫_M ch(σ(D)) Td(TM ⊗ ℂ), where σ(D) ∈ K(T*M) is the symbol class of D, ch is the Chern character, and Td is the Todd class of the complexified tangent bundle. This formula unifies the Gauss–Bonnet theorem, the Hirzebruch signature theorem, and the Riemann–Roch theorem for complex manifolds.

The proof proceeds by reducing to the case of the Dirac operator on a spinᶜ manifold using the Thom isomorphism in K‑theory and the Bott periodicity theorem. The heat kernel proof, due to Patodi, Gilkey, and Atiyah–Bott–Patodi, computes the supertrace of the heat kernel e-tD*D - e-tDD* and shows its small‑t asymptotics localize to the integral of the index density. The local index theorem identifies the t⁰ coefficient with the characteristic form ch(σ(D)) Td(TM ⊗ ℂ).

Applications are vast: the index of the Dolbeault operator ∂̄ on a complex manifold gives the holomorphic Euler characteristic Σ (-1)^q dim Hp,q; the index of the signature operator gives the signature of the intersection form; the index of the Dirac operator on a spin manifold gives the Â‑genus. In gauge theory, the index of the Dirac operator coupled to a Yang–Mills connection computes the number of fermion zero modes, which determines anomalies via the Atiyah–Singer index theorem for families.

Geometric Quantization and Symplectic Topology

Geometric quantization constructs a Hilbert space from a symplectic manifold (M,ω) representing the phase space of a classical system. The prequantization step requires a complex line bundle L → M with connection ∇ whose curvature is -iω; this exists iff the cohomology class [ω/2π] is integral (the Bohr–Sommerfeld condition). Sections of L form the prequantum Hilbert space with inner product ⟨s₁,s₂⟩ = ∫_M h(s₁,s₂) ωⁿ/n!, where h is the Hermitian metric on L.

Polarization selects a Lagrangian subbundle P ⊂ TM ⊗ ℂ (e.g., a Kähler polarization given by a compatible complex structure J). The quantum Hilbert space consists of covariantly constant sections along P: ∇_X s = 0 for X ∈ P. For a Kähler polarization, these are holomorphic sections of L, and the quantum space is the space of holomorphic sections H⁰(M, L). The dimension of this space, given by the Riemann–Roch–Hirzebruch formula, equals the symplectic volume ∫_M ωⁿ/n! plus curvature corrections.

In symplectic topology, the moment map for a Hamiltonian group action μ: M → 𝔤* allows symplectic reduction: the reduced space M//G = μ-1(0)/G inherits a symplectic form. The Guillemin–Sternberg “quantization commutes with reduction” theorem states that the quantization of the reduced space equals the G‑invariant part of the quantization of M. This principle underlies the geometric construction of representations of compact Lie groups via the Borel–Weil–Bott theorem, where M = G/T is a flag manifold, ω is the Kirillov–Kostant–Souriau form, and quantization yields irreducible representations with highest weight determined by the integral coadjoint orbit.

  • Confusing the heat kernel expansion coefficients with the full heat trace; only the integrated coefficients give topological invariants.
  • Assuming every characteristic class can be represented by a Chern–Weil form without checking the bundle admits a connection (always true for smooth bundles, but the form depends on the connection).
  • Forgetting that a spin structure requires w₂ = 0; many manifolds (e.g., ℂP²) are not spin, so the Dirac operator does not exist without a spinᶜ structure.
  • Misapplying the Atiyah–Singer formula by using the wrong Todd class or Chern character for the symbol class of the operator.
  • Neglecting the integrality condition [ω/2π] ∈ H²(M;ℤ) in geometric quantization; without it the prequantum line bundle does not exist.
  • Treating the moment map as a globally defined function on the reduced space; it is only defined on the level set and descends after quotient.
  • Overlooking that the index of a twisted Dirac operator involves the Chern character of the twisting bundle, not just its rank.

These advanced topics connect analysis, topology, and physics, and mastery of their precise statements is essential for solving high‑level problems.

hand/quantum-field-theory.html:
Path Integral Formulation and Functional Methods

The path integral provides a formulation of quantum field theory that is manifestly Lorentz invariant and naturally suited for gauge theories and perturbation theory. Instead of canonical operators, one integrates over all field configurations weighted by the exponential of i times the action. For a real scalar field the generating functional is Z[J] = ∫𝒟φ exp{i∫d⁴x[½(∂μφ)(∂μφ) − ½m²φ² − V(φ) + Jφ]}. Functional differentiation with respect to the source J yields time‑ordered correlation functions: ⟨0|T{φ(x₁)…φ(xₙ)}|0⟩ = (−i)ⁿ δⁿZ[J]/δJ(x₁)…δJ(xₙ) evaluated at J = 0. The connected generating functional W[J] = −i ln Z[J] produces connected Green functions, while the effective action Γ[φ_cl] obtained by Legendre transformation of W[J] is the generator of one‑particle‑irreducible (1PI) vertices. In gauge theories the Faddeev–Popov procedure introduces ghost fields to fix the gauge redundancy; the resulting functional integral includes a determinant that can be represented by anticommuting scalar fields. The background field method splits the gauge field into a classical background and a quantum fluctuation, preserving gauge invariance of the effective action and simplifying the computation of the beta function. Functional determinants are evaluated using ζ‑function regularisation or heat‑kernel techniques, leading to the well‑known one‑loop effective potential for scalar fields and the Coleman–Weinberg potential. The path integral also underlies the derivation of the Schwinger–Dyson equations, which are the quantum equations of motion for Green functions, and the Ward–Takahashi identities that encode gauge symmetry at the quantum level.

Renormalization Group and Effective Field Theories

The renormalization group (RG) describes how the parameters of a quantum field theory change with the energy scale at which the theory is probed. Wilson’s momentum‑shell integration provides a physical picture: high‑momentum modes are integrated out, generating an effective action for the remaining low‑momentum fields. The flow of couplings is governed by beta functions β(g) = μ∂g/∂μ. In a renormalizable theory only a finite number of couplings run; in an effective field theory (EFT) an infinite tower of higher‑dimensional operators appears, suppressed by powers of a heavy scale Λ. The Standard Model viewed as an EFT includes dimension‑six operators such as (H†H)³/Λ² that parametrise possible new physics. The Callan–Symanzik equation, (μ∂/∂μ + β(g)∂/∂g + nγ) G⁽ⁿ⁾ = 0, resums leading logarithms and yields scaling behaviour near fixed points. Asymptotic freedom in QCD follows from the negative one‑loop beta function β(g) = −(11 − 2/3 n_f) g³/(16π²), where n_f is the number of active quark flavours. Conversely, the QED beta function β(e) = e³/(12π²) is positive, so the electromagnetic coupling grows at high energy. The RG improved effective potential resums large logarithms in the Higgs sector, stabilising the electroweak vacuum up to the Planck scale for the measured Higgs mass. Matching and running between different EFTs (e.g. integrating out the top quark, W, Z, and Higgs) is performed at successive thresholds, ensuring continuity of Green functions. Lattice simulations provide non‑perturbative checks of RG flow, confirming the existence of a continuum limit for asymptotically free theories.

Worked Example: One‑Loop Beta Function in QCD
Compute the one‑loop beta function for an SU(N) gauge theory with n_f Dirac fermions in the fundamental representation.
The gauge boson self‑energy receives contributions from the gluon loop, the ghost loop, and the fermion loop. Using dimensional regularisation in d = 4 − ε dimensions, the divergent part of the gluon vacuum polarisation is Πabμν(q) = δab(q_μ q_ν − q² gμν) (g²/(16π²)) (1/ε) [ (11/3) C_A − (4/3) T_R n_f ], where C_A = N for SU(N) and T_R = 1/2. The counterterm for the gauge coupling is δg = − (g³/(16π²)) (1/ε) [ (11/3) C_A − (4/3) T_R n_f ]. The beta function follows from β(g) = −ε g + g ∂δg/∂g, yielding β(g) = − g³/(16π²) [ (11/3) C_A − (4/3) T_R n_f ]. For QCD with N = 3, C_A = 3, T_R = 1/2, this becomes β(g) = − g³/(16π²) (11 − 2/3 n_f). The negative sign for n_f ≤ 16 confirms asymptotic freedom.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for the sign of the beta function, first identify the gauge group and matter content. Remember that gauge boson loops give a positive contribution to the coefficient (screening) while fermion loops give a negative contribution (antiscreening). For SU(N) with n_f flavours, the coefficient is (11/3)C_A − (4/3)T_R n_f. Quick mental arithmetic: for QCD, 11 − 2/3 n_f; if n_f = 6 the coefficient is 7, still negative. Write the final beta function as β(g) = −b₀ g³/(16π²) with b₀ > 0 for asymptotic freedom.

Anomalies and Ward Identities

Classical symmetries that cannot be preserved upon quantisation are called anomalies. The most famous is the axial (chiral) anomaly in four‑dimensional gauge theories. For a massless Dirac fermion coupled to a U(1) gauge field, the classical axial current J^μ5 = ψ̄γ^μγ5ψ satisfies ∂_μ J^μ5 = 0. At one loop the triangle diagram with two vector currents and one axial current yields a non‑zero divergence: ∂_μ J^μ5 = (e²/(16π²)) εμνρσ Fμν Fρσ. The coefficient is fixed by the Adler–Bell–Jackiw calculation and is independent of the regularisation scheme, reflecting its topological nature. In non‑Abelian gauge theories the anomaly appears in the divergence of the singlet axial current and in the gauge current itself if the fermion representation is chiral. Cancellation of gauge anomalies imposes strong constraints on the fermion content of the Standard Model: the sum of charges over all left‑handed fermions must vanish, which is satisfied by the quark‑lepton generation structure. The Ward–Takahashi identities are the quantum counterparts of Noether’s theorem; they relate Green functions with an insertion of the divergence of a current to contact terms. For a vector current in QED the identity reads q_μ Γ^μ(p',p) = S-1(p') − S-1(p), guaranteeing the photon remains massless. In the presence of an anomaly the Ward identity acquires an extra term proportional to the anomaly coefficient, leading to the non‑conservation of the axial current. The ’t Hooft anomaly matching condition states that the anomaly computed in the ultraviolet theory must equal that in the infrared effective theory, providing a powerful check on proposed low‑energy dynamics such as chiral symmetry breaking in QCD.

Non‑Perturbative Methods: Instantons and Lattice QCD

Perturbation theory expands around the trivial vacuum and cannot capture tunnelling between topologically distinct vacua. In Yang–Mills theory the gauge field configurations are classified by the Pontryagin index Q = (1/32π²) ∫ d⁴x εμνρσ Tr(FμνFρσ), an integer. Instantons are finite‑action solutions of the Euclidean equations of motion with Q = ±1; the single instanton in SU(2) has action S_inst = 8π²/g² and size ρ. The instanton contribution to the path integral is weighted by exp(−8π²/g²) and generates an effective ’t Hooft vertex that violates the axial U(1) symmetry, providing a microscopic explanation for the η′ mass. Multi‑instanton configurations and instanton–anti‑instanton molecules are believed to drive chiral symmetry breaking and confinement. Lattice QCD discretises spacetime on a hypercubic grid with spacing a, replacing the functional integral by a high‑dimensional ordinary integral over link variables U_μ(x) ∈ SU(3). The Wilson gauge action S_W = β ∑_P (1 − 1/3 Re Tr U_P) reproduces the continuum Yang–Mills action as a → 0 with β = 6/g². Fermions are introduced via the Wilson–Dirac operator or staggered fermions, avoiding the fermion doubling problem at the cost of explicit chiral symmetry breaking. Observables such as hadron masses, decay constants, and the running coupling are extracted from Euclidean correlation functions. The continuum limit is taken by extrapolating a → 0 while keeping physical quantities fixed, a procedure verified by the scaling of the string tension and the Λ parameter. Modern simulations with physical quark masses and controlled systematic errors achieve sub‑percent precision for quantities like the proton mass and the strong coupling α_s(m_Z).

Topological Defects and Solitons in Field Theory

Field theories with spontaneous symmetry breaking admit stable, finite‑energy configurations known as topological defects. The classification follows from the homotopy groups of the vacuum manifold M = G/H, where G is the original symmetry group and H the unbroken subgroup. Domain walls correspond to π₀(M) ≠ 0, cosmic strings to π₁(M) ≠ 0, monopoles to π₂(M) ≠ 0, and textures to π₃(M) ≠ 0. In a real scalar φ⁴ theory with potential V(φ) = λ/4 (φ² − v²)², the kink solution φ(x) = v tanh(m x/√2) interpolates between the two vacua φ = ±v and has mass M_kink = 2√2 m³/(3λ). The kink is a 1+1 dimensional soliton; its stability is guaranteed by the topological charge Q = (φ(+∞) − φ(−∞))/(2v) = 1. In the Abelian Higgs model (U(1) gauge theory with a complex scalar), vortex strings carry quantised magnetic flux Φ = 2π n/e, where n ∈ ℤ is the winding number. The Nielsen–Olesen vortex has a core size ∼ 1/(ev) and a tension T ∼ 2π v² for type‑II superconductors (λ > e²). ’t Hooft–Polyakov monopoles arise in an SU(2) gauge theory broken to U(1) by an adjoint scalar triplet; the monopole mass is M_mon = 4π v/e times a function of λ/e². These monopoles carry magnetic charge g = 4π/e and satisfy the Dirac quantisation condition eg = 2π n. In supersymmetric theories, BPS solitons saturate a Bogomol’nyi bound, making their masses exactly calculable and protected from quantum corrections. Topological defects play a crucial role in cosmology (e.g., cosmic strings as seeds for structure formation) and in condensed matter analogues such as vortices in superfluid helium and domain walls in ferromagnets.

  • Confusing the sign of the beta function: gauge boson loops give antiscreening (negative contribution to β), fermion loops give screening (positive contribution).
  • Assuming all anomalies cancel automatically; gauge anomaly cancellation imposes non‑trivial constraints on fermion representations.
  • Treating instanton effects as perturbative in the coupling; they are non‑perturbative, scaling as exp(−8π²/g²).
  • Neglecting the need for matching conditions when integrating out heavy fields in an EFT; thresholds generate finite shifts in couplings.
  • Misidentifying the homotopy group that classifies a defect; domain walls need π₀, strings π₁, monopoles π₂, textures π₃.
  • Overlooking the role of the Faddeev–Popov ghosts in preserving unitarity in gauge‑fixed path integrals.
  • Using the tree‑level mass formula for solitons when quantum corrections (e.g., BPS saturation) modify the mass.
The advanced sections above complete the next‑level coverage of quantum field theory topics required for competitive examinations.
