hand/extended-tft.html:
Higher Categorical Foundations: (∞,n)-Categories and the Cobordism Category

The cobordism hypothesis is fundamentally a statement about (∞,n)-categories — higher categories where all k-morphisms for k > n are invertible and all k-morphisms for k > n+1 are identities. The symmetric monoidal (∞,n)-category Bordnfr of framed cobordisms has objects 0-manifolds, 1-morphisms 1-dimensional cobordisms, up to n-morphisms n-dimensional cobordisms with corners, and all higher morphisms given by diffeomorphisms, isotopies, and higher isotopies. The framing condition means each manifold is equipped with a trivialization of its tangent bundle plus the normal bundle in the ambient Euclidean space; this is equivalent to a map to the classifying space BSO(n) lifted to a point. The (∞,n)-categorical structure is essential because the duality data required by the cobordism hypothesis — evaluation and coevaluation maps, their adjoints, and the higher coherence isomorphisms — live naturally in this setting. An (∞,n)-category can be modeled by complete Segal spaces, Θn-spaces, or iterated complete Segal objects; Lurie's proof uses the (∞,n)-category of (∞,n)-categories itself. The symmetric monoidal structure on Bordnfr is given by disjoint union, and the unit is the empty manifold. The cobordism hypothesis asserts that Bordnfr is the free symmetric monoidal (∞,n)-category with duals on a single object — the positively framed point. This universal property means that giving a symmetric monoidal functor Z: Bordnfr → C is equivalent to giving a fully dualizable object in C. The (∞,n)-categorical language is not merely technical overhead: it captures the fact that the space of TQFTs is itself an ∞-groupoid, with equivalences, higher equivalences, and so on, reflecting the homotopical nature of the classification.

Invertible TQFTs, Anomalies, and the Cobordism Hypothesis with Singularities

An invertible TQFT is a symmetric monoidal functor Z: Bordn → C where C is a symmetric monoidal (∞,n)-category and Z(M) is invertible for every manifold M. Invertible TQFTs correspond to homotopy maps from the cobordism category to the Picard ∞-groupoid of C — they are classified by the cohomology of the classifying space of the tangential structure. For oriented manifolds, invertible TQFTs are classified by Hn+1(BSO(n); U(1)) ≅ ℤ for n odd and ℤ/2 for n even, capturing the familiar θ-term and the Arf invariant. Anomalies in quantum field theory arise when a theory cannot be defined on a manifold without additional structure — the partition function is not a number but a section of a line bundle over the space of background fields. The anomaly is itself an invertible (n+1)-dimensional TQFT, and the anomalous n-dimensional theory lives on the boundary of this (n+1)-dimensional bulk. The cobordism hypothesis with singularities (Lurie, Ayala-Francis) extends the classification to TQFTs with defects: one specifies a stratified tangential structure where strata of codimension k are labeled by k-dualizable objects. The classification then states that TQFTs with singularities valued in C are equivalent to maps from the (∞,n)-category of singular cobordisms to C, which in turn are determined by a choice of fully dualizable objects for each stratum satisfying compatibility conditions. This framework recovers the classification of topological phases of matter with symmetry: symmetry-protected topological (SPT) phases correspond to invertible TQFTs with a background gauge field for the symmetry group G, classified by the cobordism group Ωn+1G or the group cohomology Hn+1(G; U(1)) for finite G. The Freed-Hopkins theorem identifies the classification of reflection-positive invertible TQFTs with the Anderson dual of the spin cobordism spectrum, providing a complete classification of fermionic SPT phases.

Worked Example: Classifying 2D Invertible TQFTs with Spin Structure
Determine the group of deformation classes of 2-dimensional invertible spin TQFTs. Explain how this relates to the Arf invariant and the classification of fermionic SPT phases in 1+1 dimensions.
A 2-dimensional invertible spin TQFT is a symmetric monoidal functor Z: Bord2spin → Vectℂ (or the Picard ∞-groupoid of Vectℂ). By the cobordism hypothesis with singularities, such TQFTs are classified by the spin cobordism group Ω3spin (since invertible n-dimensional TQFTs correspond to Ωn+1). The spin cobordism groups are known: Ω0spin = ℤ, Ω1spin = ℤ/2, Ω2spin = ℤ/2, Ω3spin = 0, Ω4spin = ℤ. Thus Ω3spin = 0, meaning there are no non-trivial 2D invertible spin TQFTs up to deformation. However, the classification of 1+1D fermionic SPT phases with spin structure is given by Ω2spin = ℤ/2. The non-trivial element is the Arf invariant TQFT: on a closed spin surface Σ, Z(Σ) = (-1)Arf(Σ) where Arf(Σ) ∈ ℤ/2 is the Arf invariant of the spin structure. This is a 2D invertible TQFT, but it is not fully extended — it does not assign data to points and 1-manifolds in a way that satisfies the full cobordism hypothesis. The fully extended version would require a 3D bulk, but Ω3spin = 0 means no such bulk exists. The resolution is that the Arf TQFT is anomalous: it lives on the boundary of a 3D invertible TQFT with a different tangential structure (pin-), or it is a relative theory. The group of 2D invertible spin TQFTs (not necessarily fully extended) is Hom(Ω2spin, U(1)) = ℤ/2, generated by the Arf invariant.
Exam Strategy: Cobordism Groups and Anomaly Classification
When asked to classify invertible TQFTs or anomalies in dimension n, compute the relevant cobordism group Ωn+1structure or the cohomology group Hn+1(B(structure); U(1)). Memorize low-dimensional spin and oriented cobordism groups: Ω0SO=ℤ, Ω1SO=0, Ω2SO=0, Ω3SO=0, Ω4SO=ℤ; Ω0spin=ℤ, Ω1spin=ℤ/2, Ω2spin=ℤ/2, Ω3spin=0, Ω4spin=ℤ. The Arf invariant generates Ω2spin; the signature generates Ω4SO. For finite group symmetries, use group cohomology Hn+1(G; U(1)). Distinguish between fully extended TQFTs (classified by Ωn+1) and non-extended ones (classified by Hom(Ωn, U(1))).

Factorization Homology and the Local-to-Global Principle

Factorization homology (also called topological chiral homology) provides a framework for constructing and understanding extended TQFTs that generalizes the state-sum approach. Given an En-algebra A in a symmetric monoidal (∞,1)-category C (typically chain complexes or spectra), factorization homology assigns to each n-manifold M an object ∫M A ∈ C, defined as a colimit over the Ran space of M of the factorization algebra associated to A. For a framed n-manifold, the factorization homology of an En-algebra recovers the value of the corresponding fully extended TQFT on M. The cobordism hypothesis in this language states that the (∞,n)-category of En-algebras in C is equivalent to the (∞,n)-category of fully extended TQFTs Bordnfr → C. The local-to-global principle asserts that the value of the TQFT on a manifold M can be computed by decomposing M into simpler pieces (e.g., handlebodies, simplices) and gluing the corresponding algebraic data — this is the higher-categorical analogue of the Atiyah-Segal gluing axioms. For n=2, an E2-algebra is a braided monoidal category, and factorization homology on a surface Σ computes the space of conformal blocks of the associated 2D CFT. For n=3, an E3-algebra is a symmetric monoidal category, and factorization homology on a 3-manifold M recovers the Turaev-Viro or Reshetikhin-Turaev invariant depending on the choice of E3-algebra (a fusion category or a modular tensor category). The factorization homology perspective clarifies the relationship between different constructions: the Turaev-Viro TQFT arises from the E3-algebra given by the Drinfeld center Z(C) of a fusion category C, while the Reshetikhin-Turaev TQFT arises from a modular tensor category viewed as an E3-algebra. The gluing formula for factorization homology expresses the value on a manifold cut along a hypersurface as a coend (or homotopy coend) over the category assigned to the hypersurface, generalizing the state-sum gluing of 6j-symbols.

Boundary Conditions, Defects, and the Classification of Gapped Phases

Extended TQFTs naturally incorporate boundary conditions and defects as part of their data. A boundary condition for an n-dimensional TQFT Z: Bordn → C is a symmetric monoidal functor from the (∞,n)-category of manifolds with boundary to C that restricts to Z on the interior. In the cobordism hypothesis framework, boundary conditions correspond to modules over the fully dualizable object Z(pt+) — specifically, a boundary condition is a 1-morphism from the unit object to Z(pt+) in C, or equivalently a left module over Z(pt+). Domain walls between two TQFTs Z1 and Z2 correspond to bimodules between the corresponding fully dualizable objects. Point defects (codimension n) correspond to objects in the higher Morita category, line defects (codimension n-1) to 1-morphisms, and so on. The classification of gapped phases of matter with symmetry G in n spatial dimensions is given by the (∞,n)-category of TQFTs with a map to BG (the classifying space of G), or equivalently by the (∞,n)-category of G-equivariant fully dualizable objects. For invertible phases (SPT phases), this reduces to the cobordism group Ωn+1G or the group cohomology Hn+1(G; U(1)) for finite G. For non-invertible phases (topological order), the classification involves fusion categories (for 2+1D) and braided fusion categories (for 3+1D). The bulk-boundary correspondence states that a gapped boundary of a topological phase corresponds to a Lagrangian algebra (or condensable algebra) in the modular tensor category describing the bulk anyons. The anyon condensation procedure — passing from a modular tensor category C to a fusion category CA of modules over a condensable algebra A — describes the transition between topological phases. The Walker-Wang models provide a lattice realization of 3+1D topological phases with loop-like excitations, classified by braided fusion categories. The classification of 2+1D fermionic topological orders uses spin modular tensor categories (or super-modular categories), where the transparent fermion ψ satisfies ψ ⊗ ψ = 1 and has twist θψ = -1. The 16-fold way classifies fermionic topological orders with a given chiral central charge c- mod 8.

The Proof Strategy: Morse Theory, Cerf Theory, and Handlebody Decompositions

The proof of the cobordism hypothesis (Lurie, 2009) proceeds by analyzing the (∞,n)-category Bordnfr through the lens of Morse theory and handlebody decompositions. A framed manifold admits a Morse function with critical points of index 0 through n; each critical point corresponds to a handle attachment, and the framed structure provides a trivialization of the normal bundle of the attaching sphere. The (∞,n)-category Bordnfr is generated by the elementary cobordisms corresponding to handle attachments: the 0-handle (a disk), the 1-handle (a pair of pants), up to the n-handle. The relations among these generators come from Cerf theory — the study of 1-parameter families of Morse functions. Cerf's theorem states that any two Morse functions on a manifold are connected by a path that passes through only birth-death singularities (where a pair of critical points of adjacent index cancel) and handle slides. These singularities correspond precisely to the duality relations in the (∞,n)-category: the birth of a k-handle and (k+1)-handle pair corresponds to the coevaluation map, their death to the evaluation map, and handle slides to the higher coherence isomorphisms. The framed condition ensures that the space of framings of the attaching spheres is contractible, so there are no additional obstructions. The proof then shows that the (∞,n)-category presented by these generators and relations satisfies the universal property of the free symmetric monoidal (∞,n)-category with duals on one object. The key technical tool is the (∞,n)-category of (∞,n)-categories, where one constructs a map from the presented category to any target C by inductively choosing duals for the image of the point. The induction proceeds by dimension: at step k, one has defined the functor on k-manifolds and must extend to (k+1)-manifolds by providing the (k+1)-duality data. The contractibility of the space of choices at each step follows from the fact that the space of framed embeddings of a k-sphere into a (k+1)-manifold is connected. For non-framed tangential structures (oriented, spin, etc.), one must take the homotopy quotient by the action of the orthogonal group, which introduces the homotopy fixed point data corresponding to the action of SO(n) on the fully dualizable object.

  • Confusing the classification of fully extended TQFTs (cobordism hypothesis: fully dualizable objects) with non-extended TQFTs (Atiyah-Segal: Frobenius algebras for n=2, modular tensor categories for n=3).
  • Assuming all dualizable objects are fully dualizable — in higher categories, an object can be dualizable but fail to have higher adjoints (e.g., a fusion category that is not spherical).
  • Mixing up the dimension shift: invertible n-dimensional TQFTs are classified by Ωn+1, not Ωn.
  • Treating the Arf invariant as a fully extended 2D spin TQFT — it is not fully extended; it is anomalous and requires a 3D bulk with pin- structure.
  • Confusing En-algebras with n-dualizable objects — an En-algebra in C corresponds to a fully extended TQFT valued in C, but the object assigned to the point is the En-algebra itself viewed as an object in the Morita (∞,n)-category of En-algebras.
  • Overlooking the role of the Serre functor and Nakayama automorphism in the classification of TQFTs with anomalies — these appear when the target category is not symmetric monoidal but only braided or has a non-trivial twist.
  • Assuming the Turaev-Viro and Reshetikhin-Turaev TQFTs are distinct for the same input — for a modular tensor category C, the Turaev-Viro TQFT of the Drinfeld center Z(C) is equivalent to the Reshetikhin-Turaev TQFT of C ⊠ Crev.

hand/lie-theory.html:
Cartan Subalgebras, Root Space Decomposition and the Role of Regular Elements

For a finite‑dimensional Lie algebra 𝔤 over an algebraically closed field of characteristic 0, a Cartan subalgebra 𝔥 is a maximal nilpotent subalgebra that equals its own normaliser. In the complex semisimple case 𝔥 is automatically abelian and consists of semisimple elements. The adjoint action of 𝔥 on 𝔤 yields the root space decomposition:

𝔤 = 𝔥 ⊕ ⨁α∈Δ 𝔤α, where 𝔤α= { X∈𝔤 | [H,X]=α(H)X for all H∈𝔥 }.

The set Δ⊂𝔥* of non‑zero weights is the root system. Each root space 𝔤α is one‑dimensional for simple Lie algebras, and the Killing form B provides an identification 𝔥≅𝔥* via B(H,·). This identification lets us define the coroot α∨=2α/⟨α,α⟩, which plays a central part in the Weyl group action.

A regular element H∈𝔥 satisfies α(H)≠0 for every root α. Regular elements are dense in 𝔥 and their centraliser in 𝔤 is exactly 𝔥. Consequently, the adjoint orbit of a regular semisimple element is of maximal dimension, equal to dim 𝔤−rank 𝔤. This fact underlies the construction of the Chevalley basis, where one chooses root vectors Eα∈𝔤α satisfying [Eα,E−α]=α∨ and the Serre relations:

ad(Eα)1−⟨β,α∨⟩(Eβ)=0 for α≠β.

These relations generate the universal enveloping algebra U(𝔤) and are the algebraic backbone of the highest‑weight theory presented earlier. In practice, exam‑writers often ask candidates to exhibit the root diagram of a low‑rank algebra (e.g., A₂ or B₂) and to identify the corresponding Cartan subalgebra, simple roots, and fundamental weights. Mastery of the geometric picture—hyperplanes defined by α(H)=0 partitioning 𝔥ℝ into Weyl chambers—allows quick deduction of dominant weights and the action of the Weyl group.

Jacobson‑Morozov Theorem, Nilpotent Orbits and the Bala‑Carter Classification

The Jacobson‑Morozov theorem asserts that every non‑zero nilpotent element e∈𝔤 can be embedded in an sl₂‑triple (e,h,f) satisfying

[h,e]=2e, [h,f]=−2f, [e,f]=h.

This embedding is unique up to conjugacy by the centraliser of e. The theorem provides a bridge between the geometry of nilpotent orbits—adjoint orbits of nilpotent elements—and the representation theory of sl₂, because the adjoint action of the triple decomposes 𝔤 into eigenspaces of ad h with integer eigenvalues.

Nilpotent orbits in a complex semisimple Lie algebra are partially ordered by closure inclusion. The Bala‑Carter classification labels each orbit by a pair (𝔩,𝔬𝔩) where 𝔩 is a Levi subalgebra and 𝔬𝔩 is a distinguished nilpotent orbit in 𝔩. For classical types the classification reduces to partitions of n with parity constraints (e.g., for 𝔰𝔬2n+1 the partitions must have even parts occurring with even multiplicity). For exceptional algebras the labels are given by weighted Dynkin diagrams, where each node carries a number 0,1 or 2 indicating the eigenvalue of h on the corresponding simple root space.

In examinations, a common task is to determine the dimension of a nilpotent orbit. The dimension formula

dim 𝒪e=dim 𝔤−dim 𝔤e,

where 𝔤e is the centraliser of e, can be evaluated using the weighted Dynkin diagram: the number of 2’s gives dim 𝔤e∩𝔫+, the number of 1’s gives dim 𝔤e∩𝔥, etc. For instance, in 𝔰𝔩4 the nilpotent orbit corresponding to the partition (3,1) has weighted diagram (2,0,0) and dimension 12.

The Springer correspondence further links nilpotent orbits to irreducible representations of the Weyl group, a topic that appears in advanced combinatorial questions. Understanding the Jacobson‑Morozov construction also aids in the study of parabolic subalgebras, because the element h defines a grading 𝔤=⊕i∈ℤ𝔤(i) with 𝔤(0) a reductive Levi factor and 𝔤(>0) the nilradical of a parabolic.

Technique: Using Weighted Dynkin Diagrams to Compute Orbit Dimensions
In 𝔰𝔬8, consider the nilpotent element whose weighted Dynkin diagram is (2,1,0,0). Determine the dimension of its adjoint orbit.

Step 1: Identify the grading defined by h. The numbers on the diagram give the eigenvalues of h on the simple root spaces: α₁→2, α₂→1, α₃→0, α₄→0.

Step 2: Compute dim 𝔤e. The centraliser consists of the Cartan subalgebra elements commuting with h (those with eigenvalue 0) and the root spaces whose roots have zero pairing with h. Counting roots of 𝔰𝔬8 (24 roots) and noting that roots with coefficient sum zero under h are those orthogonal to (2,1,0,0), we find 8 such roots.

Step 3: Add the dimension of the Cartan subalgebra (rank 4) that lies in the zero eigenspace, giving dim 𝔤e=8+4=12.

Step 4: Use dim 𝔤=28 for 𝔰𝔬8. Hence dim 𝒪e=28−12=16.

Thus the nilpotent orbit has dimension 16.

Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for the dimension of a nilpotent orbit, first write down the weighted Dynkin diagram, then count zero‑eigenvalue roots rather than attempting a full centraliser computation. This reduces the problem to a quick root‑counting exercise that can be done within a minute.

Satake Diagrams, Real Forms of Complex Lie Algebras and Their Physical Significance

Real forms of a complex semisimple Lie algebra 𝔤ℂ are classified by involutive automorphisms σ:𝔤ℂ→𝔤ℂ with fixed point set 𝔤ℝ=𝔤ℂσ. Satake diagrams encode σ by decorating the Dynkin diagram of 𝔤ℂ: nodes fixed by σ are painted black (compact roots), while pairs of nodes exchanged by σ are connected by a curved arrow. The resulting diagram uniquely determines the real form up to isomorphism.

For example, the complex algebra 𝔰𝔩4(ℂ) has three non‑compact real forms:

  • 𝔰𝔩4(ℝ) – the split form, corresponding to a Satake diagram with all nodes white and no arrows.
  • 𝔰𝔲(2,2) – a non‑compact form with two black nodes (the compact simple roots) and two white nodes.
  • 𝔰𝔲(4) – the compact real form, represented by a diagram with all nodes black.

The classification proceeds by first choosing a Cartan involution θ, then decomposing 𝔤ℝ=𝔨⊕𝔭 (Cartan decomposition). The restricted root system Σ⊂𝔞*, where 𝔞 is a maximal abelian subspace of 𝔭, governs the Iwasawa decomposition G=KAN. In the split case Σ coincides with the original root system Δ, while in non‑split forms Σ may be of lower rank, leading to different Weyl groups (the restricted Weyl group).

Physical applications often hinge on the signature of the invariant bilinear form. The Lorentz algebra 𝔰𝔬(3,1) is a real form of 𝔰𝔬4(ℂ) with Satake diagram having one black node and one white node connected by an arrow, reflecting the mixed compact‑non‑compact nature of rotations versus boosts. Similarly, the conformal algebra in four dimensions, 𝔰𝔬(4,2), appears as a real form of 𝔰𝔬6(ℂ) with a Satake diagram indicating two compact and two non‑compact simple roots.

Exam questions may present a Satake diagram and ask for the corresponding real Lie algebra, its maximal compact subalgebra 𝔨, or the dimension of the non‑compact part 𝔭. The standard procedure is:

  1. Identify black nodes → compact simple roots → generate 𝔨.
  2. Identify white nodes and arrows → determine how many simple roots are non‑compact and which are paired.
  3. Compute rank 𝔞 as the number of white nodes not paired by an arrow.
  4. Use dim 𝔤=dim 𝔨+dim 𝔭 with dim 𝔭=dim 𝔞+|Σ+|·dim 𝔫, where 𝔫 is the nilpotent part generated by positive restricted roots.

Understanding Satake diagrams also clarifies why certain gauge groups are admissible in supergravity theories: the scalar manifolds are often symmetric spaces G/K with G a non‑compact real form and K its maximal compact subgroup. The classification of possible G/K is directly read off from the list of Satake diagrams.

Cohomology of Lie Groups, Borel–Weil–Bott Theory and Geometric Realisation of Representations

The cohomology ring H*(G;ℝ) of a compact connected Lie group G is an exterior algebra generated by odd‑degree classes corresponding to the primitive elements of the Hopf algebra structure. Explicitly, if rank G=r and the exponents of the Weyl group are m₁,…,mr, then

H*(G;ℝ) ≅ Λ(ω₁, …, ωr), deg ωi=2mi+1.

This description follows from the Leray–Serre spectral sequence of the fibration G→EG→BG and the fact that BG has polynomial cohomology ℝ[c₁,…,cr] with deg ci=2(mi+1).

The Borel–Weil–Bott theorem provides a geometric construction of every irreducible finite‑dimensional representation V(λ) of a complex semisimple Lie group Gℂ. For a dominant integral weight λ, one considers the holomorphic line bundle Lλ over the flag variety Gℂ/B. The theorem states:

  • If λ+ρ is regular, there exists a unique w∈W such that μ=w(λ+ρ)−ρ is dominant; then Hℓ(w)(Gℂ/B, Lλ)≅V(μ) and all other cohomology groups vanish.
  • If λ+ρ is singular, all cohomology groups are zero.

In the compact real form K⊂Gℂ, the same line bundles restrict to K‑equivariant bundles on K/T, where T is a maximal torus. The Dolbeault cohomology of these bundles yields the same representations, now realised as spaces of harmonic forms. This perspective is crucial for understanding the Peter–Weyl theorem, which asserts that L2(K) decomposes as a Hilbert direct sum ⊕λ V(λ)⊗V(λ)*.

For exam purposes, a typical problem asks to compute the Betti numbers of a flag variety or to determine which cohomology group carries a given representation. The steps are:

  1. Identify the weight λ and compute λ+ρ.
  2. Check regularity: λ+ρ lies on a wall of the Weyl chamber iff some ⟨λ+ρ,α∨⟩=0.
  3. Find the minimal w∈W sending λ+ρ to the dominant chamber; ℓ(w) gives the cohomological degree.
  4. Conclude that Hℓ(w)(G/B, Lλ)≅V(w·λ) and all other Hq=0.

As an illustration, for G=SL(3,ℂ) and λ=ω₁ (the first fundamental weight), λ+ρ=ω₁+ω₂+ω₁+ω₂=2ω₁+2ω₂ is regular; the identity element w=e works, ℓ(e)=0, so H0(G/B, Lω₁)≅V(ω₁), the standard 3‑dimensional representation. If λ=−ω₁, then λ+ρ lies on a wall, all cohomology vanishes, reflecting the fact that negative dominant weights do not yield holomorphic sections.

Quantum Groups, q‑Deformations and Their Link to Classical Lie Theory

Quantum groups emerged from the study of exactly solvable models in statistical mechanics and the theory of quantum inverse scattering. Formally, a quantum group Uq(𝔤) is a Hopf algebra deformation of the universal enveloping algebra U(𝔤) depending on a parameter q∈ℂ×. When q is not a root of unity, the representation theory of Uq(𝔤) closely mirrors that of 𝔤: simple modules are still indexed by dominant integral weights, and the characters are given by the same Weyl formula with q‑numbers replacing integers.

The defining relations are deformed Chevalley‑Serre relations. For simple roots αi, the generators Ei,Fi,Ki±1 satisfy

KiEjKi-1=q⟨αi,αj∨⟩Ej, KiFjKi-1=q-⟨αi,αj∨⟩Fj,

[Ei,Fj]=δij(Ki-Ki-1)/(q-q-1),

and the q‑Serre relations

∑k=01-⟨αj,αi∨⟩ (-1)k begin{bmatrix}1-⟨αj,αi∨⟩ kend{bmatrix}q Ei 1-⟨αj,αi∨⟩-kEjEi k=0, i≠j,

with analogous relations for the Fi. The q‑binomial coefficients encode the deformation.

When q is a primitive ℓ‑th root of unity, the representation theory changes dramatically: the center of Uq(𝔤) enlarges, leading to a finite‑dimensional quotient called the small quantum group uq(𝔤). Its simple modules are still labelled by weights modulo ℓ times the root lattice, and the category becomes non‑semisimple. This phenomenon is the algebraic underpinning of modular tensor categories used in topological quantum field theory.

Exam‑level questions may ask to write the q‑analogue of a simple commutator, to compute the dimension of a highest‑weight module at a root of unity, or to explain why the quantum determinant in Uq(𝔰𝔩n) remains central. A concise answer should mention the role of the R‑matrix, the braid group action on tensor products, and the fact that at generic q the category of finite‑dimensional Uq(𝔤)‑modules is braided and ribbon, providing a categorical framework for knot invariants such as the Jones polynomial.

  • Confusing the Cartan subalgebra of a real form with that of its complexification; always specify the field.
  • Treating a weighted Dynkin diagram as a Dynkin diagram; the numbers 0,1,2 carry grading information essential for nilpotent orbit calculations.
  • Assuming every nilpotent orbit dimension can be read off directly from the partition; for orthogonal and symplectic algebras extra parity conditions apply.
  • Neglecting the effect of singular λ+ρ in the Borel–Weil–Bott theorem; singular weights give vanishing cohomology, a frequent source of mistakes.
  • Using the undeformed Serre relations when working with quantum groups; the q‑Serre relations must replace them.
  • Overlooking the role of arrows in Satake diagrams; they indicate non‑compact simple roots that are interchanged, not mere decorative elements.
  • Mixing up the dimensions of the compact part 𝔨 and the non‑compact part 𝔭 in a Cartan decomposition; the rank of the symmetric space equals dim 𝔞, not dim 𝔭.

hand/stochastic-proc.html:
Stochastic Filtering and the Kalman-Bucy Filter

Stochastic filtering addresses the problem of estimating an unobserved signal process Xt from noisy observations Yt. The classical setup: the signal follows a diffusion dXt = b(Xt)dt + σ(Xt)dWt, while observations are dYt = h(Xt)dt + dVt, where W and V are independent Brownian motions. The filtering problem asks for the conditional distribution πt(dx) = P(Xt ∈ dx | ℱtY), where ℱtY is the observation σ-algebra. The Kushner-Stratonovich equation governs the evolution of the unnormalized conditional density ρt: dρt = L*ρtdt + ρthdYt, where L* is the adjoint of the signal generator. For linear-Gaussian systems — b(x) = Ax, σ constant, h(x) = Cx — the conditional distribution remains Gaussian, fully characterized by its mean m̂t and covariance Pt. The Kalman-Bucy filter gives the optimal estimator: dm̂t = Am̂tdt + PtCT(dYt − Cm̂tdt), with Pt satisfying the Riccati equation dPt/dt = APt + PtAT + σσT − PtCTCPt. The innovation process dIt = dYt − Cm̂tdt is a Brownian motion under the physical measure — a fundamental result linking filtering to martingale theory. For nonlinear systems, the conditional density is infinite-dimensional; particle filters (sequential Monte Carlo) approximate πt by a weighted empirical measure, resampling to combat weight degeneracy. The Zakai equation provides a linear (unnormalized) evolution for the conditional density, enabling numerical solution via finite-element or spectral methods. Filtering theory underpins target tracking, financial volatility estimation, and neural decoding — wherever a hidden state must be inferred from noisy continuous-time data.

Stochastic Optimal Control and the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman Equation

Stochastic optimal control seeks a policy ut = α(t, Xt) minimizing a cost functional J(α) = E[∫0T f(t, Xt, α(t, Xt))dt + g(XT)], where the state evolves as dXt = b(t, Xt, ut)dt + σ(t, Xt, ut)dWt. The value function V(t, x) = infα E[∫tT f(s, Xs, αs)ds + g(XT) | Xt = x] satisfies the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman (HJB) equation: −∂V/∂t = infu { f(t, x, u) + b(t, x, u)·∇V + ½ tr(σσT∇²V) }, with terminal condition V(T, x) = g(x). The infimum is attained at u* = argminu { f + b·∇V + ½ tr(σσT∇²V) }, yielding the optimal feedback law. For linear-quadratic problems — b = Ax + Bu, σ constant, f = xTQx + uTRu, g = xTGx — the value function is quadratic: V(t, x) = xTP(t)x, where P(t) solves the matrix Riccati differential equation −Ṗ = ATP + PA − PBR−1BTP + Q, P(T) = G. The optimal control is u* = −R−1BTP(t)x, a linear state feedback. Verification theorems guarantee that a smooth solution to the HJB equation with appropriate growth conditions indeed gives the value function and the optimal policy. When the HJB equation lacks classical solutions, viscosity solutions (Crandall-Lions) provide a robust framework: the value function is the unique viscosity solution, and optimal controls can be constructed via measurable selection. Stochastic control underpins Merton's portfolio problem (optimal investment/consumption with power utility), linear-quadratic-Gaussian (LQG) control, and stochastic differential games where multiple agents optimize competing objectives — the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman-Isaacs equation then involves a sup-inf over control pairs.

Worked Example: Merton's Portfolio Problem
An investor allocates wealth between a risk-free asset (dB = rB dt) and a risky asset (dS = μS dt + σS dW). With power utility U(x) = xγ/γ (γ < 1, γ ≠ 0) and consumption rate c, maximize E[∫0T e−ρtU(ct)dt + e−ρTU(XT)]. Derive the optimal portfolio weight π* and consumption c*.
Let X be wealth, π the fraction in the risky asset. Dynamics: dX = [rX + πX(μ−r) − c]dt + πXσ dW. HJB: 0 = supπ,c { e−ρtcγ/γ + Vt + [rX + πX(μ−r) − c]Vx + ½π²X²σ²Vxx }. Guess V(t, x) = e−ρtAxγ/γ. Then Vt = −ρV, Vx = e−ρtAxγ−1, Vxx = e−ρtA(γ−1)xγ−2. FOC for c: e−ρtcγ−1 = Vx ⇒ c* = A1/(γ−1)x. FOC for π: X(μ−r)Vx + πX²σ²Vxx = 0 ⇒ π* = −(μ−r)/(σ²(γ−1)) = (1−γ)−1(μ−r)/σ². Substitute into HJB, solve for A: A = [ρ − γr − ½γ(1−γ)−1(μ−r)²/σ²]/γ. Optimal consumption is proportional to wealth; optimal portfolio weight is constant (myopic), independent of horizon T.
Exam Strategy: HJB and Verification
When a problem asks to "find the optimal control" for a stochastic system, write down the HJB equation immediately — it earns method marks even if you cannot solve it fully. For verification, state the conditions: (1) V ∈ C1,2 solves HJB, (2) V has polynomial growth, (3) the candidate control u* is admissible and achieves the infimum. If the value function is not smooth, mention viscosity solutions — examiners reward awareness of the technical gap. For linear-quadratic problems, always check that the Riccati solution P(t) remains positive semidefinite; if it blows up, the problem is ill-posed.

Large Deviations Theory and the Freidlin-Wentzell Framework

Large deviations theory quantifies the exponential decay of probabilities of rare events. A family of random variables {Zε} satisfies a large deviation principle (LDP) with rate function I : X → [0, ∞] if for all measurable A, −infx∈A° I(x) ≤ liminfε→0 ε log P(Zε ∈ A) ≤ limsupε→0 ε log P(Zε ∈ A) ≤ −infx∈Ā I(x). The rate function I is lower semicontinuous with compact level sets. Cramér's theorem: for i.i.d. Xi with moment generating function M(θ) = E[eθX1], the sample mean Sn/n satisfies an LDP with rate function I(x) = supθ { θx − log M(θ) } (the Legendre-Fenchel transform). For small-noise diffusions dXtε = b(Xtε)dt + √ε σ(Xtε)dWt, the Freidlin-Wentzell theorem gives an LDP on C[0, T] with rate function IT(φ) = ½ ∫0T |σ−1(φ(s))(φ̇(s) − b(φ(s)))|² ds if φ is absolutely continuous with φ(0) = x, and ∞ otherwise. The quasi-potential V(x, y) = infT>0 infφ(0)=x, φ(T)=y IT(φ) governs exit times from domains: for a domain D with smooth boundary, the exit time τε = inf{t : Xtε ∉ D} satisfies limε→0 ε log E[τε] = V(x, ∂D). The most probable exit path minimizes IT — a deterministic variational problem. Varadhan's lemma connects Laplace integrals to rate functions: limε→0 ε log E[e−F(Zε)/ε] = −infx { F(x) + I(x) }. The contraction principle: if Zε satisfies an LDP with rate I and f is continuous, then f(Zε) satisfies an LDP with rate I'(y) = infx: f(x)=y I(x). Sanov's theorem gives the LDP for empirical measures of i.i.d. samples: the rate function is the relative entropy H(ν | μ) = ∫ log(dν/dμ) dν. Large deviations underpin importance sampling (exponential tilting), statistical mechanics (Gibbs measures), and queueing theory (buffer overflow probabilities).

Stochastic Partial Differential Equations and the Stochastic Heat Equation

Stochastic partial differential equations (SPDEs) describe random fields evolving in space and time. The prototypical example is the stochastic heat equation on ℝd: ∂tu = ½ Δu + ξ, where ξ is space-time white noise — a Gaussian random distribution with covariance E[ξ(t, x)ξ(s, y)] = δ(t−s)δ(x−y). The solution is a random distribution; for d = 1, it is a continuous function, but for d ≥ 2, it is a genuine distribution (not function-valued). The mild formulation uses the heat semigroup Pt = etΔ/2: u(t) = Ptu0 + ∫0t Pt−s dWs, where W is a cylindrical Wiener process on L²(ℝd). The stochastic convolution ∫0t Pt−s dWs is well-defined as an L²-valued Itô integral if ∫0t ||Ps||HS² ds < ∞, where ||·||HS is the Hilbert-Schmidt norm. For the stochastic heat equation on a bounded domain with Dirichlet boundary conditions, the eigenfunction expansion gives u(t, x) = Σk e−λktu0,kφk(x) + Σk φk(x) ∫0t e−λk(t−s) dβk(s), where βk are independent Brownian motions. The KPZ equation ∂th = ½ ∂xxh + ½ (∂xh)² + ξ models interface growth; the Cole-Hopf transform Z = eh linearizes it to the stochastic heat equation with multiplicative noise: ∂tZ = ½ ΔZ + Z ξ. Regularity structures (Hairer) and paracontrolled distributions (Gubinelli-Imkeller-Perkowski) provide solution theories for singular SPDEs where classical Itô calculus fails — the KPZ equation in d = 1 requires renormalization (subtracting infinite constants). The stochastic Navier-Stokes equations model turbulent fluids; the stochastic Allen-Cahn equation ∂tu = Δu − u³ + u + ξ describes phase separation with thermal fluctuations. SPDEs connect to quantum field theory (Euclidean φ⁴ theory), statistical mechanics (Glauber dynamics), and filtering (the Kushner-Stratonovich equation is an SPDE for the conditional density).

Concentration Inequalities for Martingales and Empirical Processes

Concentration inequalities bound the deviation of a random variable from its mean. For martingales, the Azuma-Hoeffding inequality states: if M0 = 0 and |Mk − Mk−1| ≤ ck almost surely, then P(Mn ≥ t) ≤ exp(−t² / (2 Σk=1n ck²)). The Bernstein-type inequality for martingales with bounded increments and predictable quadratic variation: if |Mk − Mk−1| ≤ K and Σk=1n E[(Mk − Mk−1)² | ℱk−1] ≤ V, then P(Mn ≥ t) ≤ exp(−t² / (2(V + Kt/3))). Freedman's inequality extends this to unbounded increments with a conditional variance bound. The method of bounded differences (McDiarmid's inequality): if f : Xn → ℝ satisfies |f(x) − f(x')| ≤ ci when x and x' differ only in coordinate i, then for independent Xi, P(f(X) − E[f(X)] ≥ t) ≤ exp(−2t² / Σi ci²). Talagrand's convex distance inequality: for product measures, P(|f − M| ≥ t) ≤ 4 exp(−t² / (4σ²)), where M is a median and σ² is a variance proxy. For empirical processes, let ℱ be a class of functions, X1, ..., Xn i.i.d., and define the empirical process Gn(f) = √n (Pn − P)f. The supremum Z = supf∈ℱ |Gn(f)| concentrates around its mean. Dudley's entropy integral bound: E[Z] ≤ C ∫0∞ √log N(ε, ℱ, L²(Pn)) dε, where N is the covering number. The Vapnik-Chervonenkis (VC) dimension controls the growth of N: if ℱ has VC dimension V, then N(ε, ℱ, L²(Pn)) ≤ (Cn/ε)V. Massart's finite class lemma: for finite ℱ, E[supf∈ℱ Gn(f)] ≤ √(2 log |ℱ|) supf ||f||∞. The Talagrand concentration inequality for empirical processes: P(Z ≥ E[Z] + t) ≤ exp(−t² / (2(σ² + 2E[Z]t/3))), where σ² = supf∈ℱ Var(f(X)). These tools underpin statistical learning theory (uniform convergence, Rademacher complexities), high-dimensional statistics (Lasso, matrix completion), and randomized algorithms (Johnson-Lindenstrauss lemma, matrix concentration).

  • Confusing the Kushner-Stratonovich and Zakai equations — the former is nonlinear and normalized; the latter is linear but unnormalized. Examiners often ask for the relationship: the normalized density is the Zakai solution divided by its integral.
  • Assuming the HJB equation always has a classical solution — viscosity solutions are the correct framework for non-smooth value functions. State the verification theorem conditions explicitly.
  • Misapplying the Freidlin-Wentzell rate function — it requires the diffusion coefficient σ to be invertible. For degenerate noise, the rate function involves a constrained minimization over paths compatible with the noise directions.
  • Treating space-time white noise as a function — it is a distribution; the stochastic heat equation solution in d ≥ 2 is not function-valued. The covariance δ(t−s)δ(x−y) is a formal expression.
  • Using Azuma-Hoeffding when Bernstein or Freedman is tighter — if the conditional variances are much smaller than the worst-case bound ck², the variance-aware inequalities give exponentially better bounds.
  • Confusing VC dimension with covering numbers — VC dimension controls the growth of covering numbers for indicator classes; for general function classes, metric entropy (log covering numbers) is the direct complexity measure.
  • Forgetting the renormalization in singular SPDEs — the KPZ equation and Φ⁴3 require subtracting infinite constants (Wick ordering). The solution theory (regularity structures, paracontrolled calculus) is built around this renormalization.

hand/solutions.html:
Temperature Dependence of Henry’s Constant and Gas Solubility in Natural Waters

Henry’s law constant KH is not a true constant; it varies systematically with temperature because the dissolution of a gas is an exothermic process for most gases. The van’t Hoff relation for the temperature dependence of an equilibrium constant applies: dln KH/d(1/T) = –ΔHsol/R, where ΔHsol is the enthalpy of solution (negative for exothermic dissolution). Consequently, a plot of ln KH versus 1/T yields a straight line whose slope gives ΔHsol. For oxygen in water at 298 K, KH ≈ 1.3 × 10³ atm · M⁻¹ and ΔHsol ≈ –12 kJ mol⁻¹; raising the temperature to 313 K roughly doubles KH, halving the dissolved O₂ concentration at a fixed partial pressure. This temperature sensitivity underpins the seasonal stratification of lakes: summer warming reduces O₂ solubility in the epilimnion, while the hypolimnion remains cold and oxygen‑rich until mixing occurs. In engineered systems, the same principle guides the design of aeration tanks in wastewater treatment; operators increase air flow or decrease water temperature to compensate for the reduced driving force at higher temperatures. The temperature effect also explains why carbonated beverages lose fizz more rapidly when stored warm: the equilibrium CO₂ pressure in the headspace rises as KH increases, driving CO₂ out of solution until a new equilibrium is reached. Accurate environmental modelling therefore requires temperature‑corrected Henry constants, often tabulated as KH(T) = KH⁰ exp[–ΔHsol/R(1/T – 1/T⁰)].

Non‑Ideal Solution Models: Margules, Van Laar, and Activity Coefficients

Real solutions deviate from Raoult’s law because intermolecular forces between unlike molecules differ from those in the pure components. The deviation is quantified by the activity coefficient γi, defined through the modified Raoult’s law: pi = γi xi p°i. For binary mixtures, two widely used empirical models are the two‑suffix Margules equation and the Van Laar equation. The symmetric Margules model writes ln γ₁ = A x₂² and ln γ₂ = A x₁², where A is a temperature‑dependent parameter that captures the magnitude of the deviation; A > 0 gives positive deviations (higher vapour pressure) and A < 0 gives negative deviations. The Van Laar model, derived from a quasi‑lattice approximation, expresses ln γ₁ = A₁₂ (1 + A₁₂ x₁/A₂₁ x₂)⁻² and a symmetric expression for ln γ₂, with two independent parameters A₁₂ and A₂₁. Both models reduce to Raoult’s law when the parameters vanish. In practice, parameters are obtained by fitting experimental vapour‑pressure data at a given temperature; the fitted values can then predict azeotropic composition and boiling‑point diagrams. For the ethanol–water system at 298 K, the Margules parameter A ≈ 1.6 reproduces the minimum‑boiling azeotrope at xₑₜₕₐₙₒₗ ≈ 0.90. More sophisticated models (Wilson, NRTL, UNIQUAC) introduce local‑composition concepts and are essential for multicomponent distillation design, but the Margules and Van Laar forms remain the pedagogical standard for illustrating how activity coefficients encode molecular‑level interactions.

Worked Example: Estimating Azeotropic Composition from Margules Parameter
A binary mixture of components 1 and 2 exhibits a symmetric Margules parameter A = 2.0 at 350 K. The pure‑component vapour pressures are p°₁ = 0.80 atm and p°₂ = 0.45 atm. Assuming the vapour phase behaves ideally, calculate the mole fraction of component 1 in the liquid at the azeotrope.
At an azeotrope the liquid and vapour compositions are equal: y₁ = x₁. Using modified Raoult’s law, y₁ p = γ₁ x₁ p°₁ and y₂ p = γ₂ x₂ p°₂. Dividing the two equations eliminates total pressure p: (y₁/y₂) = (γ₁ x₁ p°₁)/(γ₂ x₂ p°₂). With y₁ = x₁ and y₂ = x₂, this simplifies to 1 = (γ₁ p°₁)/(γ₂ p°₂). For the symmetric Margules model, ln γ₁ = A x₂² and ln γ₂ = A x₁². Substituting A = 2.0 gives γ₁ = exp(2 x₂²) and γ₂ = exp(2 x₁²). The azeotrope condition becomes exp(2 x₂²) · 0.80 = exp(2 x₁²) · 0.45. Taking natural logs: 2 x₂² + ln 0.80 = 2 x₁² + ln 0.45. Since x₂ = 1 – x₁, solve numerically. Iteration yields x₁ ≈ 0.68. Therefore the azeotropic liquid contains about 68 mol % component 1.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question provides a Margules or Van Laar parameter, first write the expressions for ln γ₁ and ln γ₂. Then apply the azeotrope condition γ₁ p°₁ = γ₂ p°₂ (for a binary system with ideal vapour). This reduces the problem to a single algebraic equation in x₁ that can be solved by iteration or by taking logarithms. Remember that symmetric Margules uses one parameter, while Van Laar uses two; the latter requires both parameters to be given.

Colligative Properties in Mixed Solvent Systems and Preferential Solvation

Colligative property equations are derived for a single solvent, but many practical solutions involve mixed solvents (e.g., water–ethanol, water–acetone). In a binary solvent mixture, the effective cryoscopic constant Kf,eff and ebullioscopic constant Kb,eff become composition‑dependent because the molar mass and enthalpy of fusion/vaporisation of the solvent mixture differ from those of the pure components. Moreover, solute particles may be preferentially solvated by one solvent component, altering the apparent number of free solute particles. Preferential solvation is quantified by the preferential solvation parameter δ1,2 = (∂ln a₁/∂ln x₂)T,P, where a₁ is the activity of the solute and x₂ the mole fraction of solvent 2. A positive δ indicates that the solute attracts solvent 2 more strongly than expected from bulk composition. This effect manifests as a deviation from the linear ΔTf = i Kf m relationship when the solvent composition changes. For example, adding NaCl to a water–methanol mixture shows a smaller freezing‑point depression than predicted by the pure‑water Kf because Na⁺ and Cl⁻ are preferentially hydrated, reducing the effective molality of “free” ions in the methanol‑rich domains. Accurate modelling therefore requires the use of solvent‑activity models (e.g., UNIFAC) to compute the solvent chemical potentials and the solute activity coefficients in the mixed solvent. In polymer science, the Flory–Huggins theory extends colligative concepts to polymer solutions, where the osmotic pressure π = (RT/V₁)[φ₂/N + χ φ₂² + …] includes the polymer volume fraction φ₂, degree of polymerisation N, and the interaction parameter χ. The second virial coefficient A₂ = (½ – χ)/V₁ links osmotic measurements to polymer‑solvent compatibility, a cornerstone of membrane separation and drug‑delivery design.

Solubility Product Manipulation: Common‑Ion Effect, pH‑Dependent Solubility, and Complexation Equilibria

The solubility product Ksp governs the equilibrium between a sparingly soluble solid and its ions, but real systems often involve additional equilibria that shift the apparent solubility. The common‑ion effect is the simplest: adding a soluble salt that shares an ion with the solid (e.g., NaCl to AgCl) raises the concentration of the common ion, forcing the dissolution equilibrium AgCl(s) ⇌ Ag⁺ + Cl⁻ to the left and decreasing the molar solubility s. Quantitatively, if the added common‑ion concentration is C, then Ksp = (s + C) s ≈ C s for C ≫ s, giving s ≈ Ksp/C. pH‑dependent solubility arises when the anion is the conjugate base of a weak acid (CO₃²⁻, S²⁻, OH⁻, PO₄³⁻). Lowering the pH protonates the anion, removing it from the solubility equilibrium and increasing dissolution. For calcium carbonate, CaCO₃(s) ⇌ Ca²⁺ + CO₃²⁻ with Ksp = 3.3 × 10⁻⁹; in acidic solution CO₃²⁻ + H⁺ ⇌ HCO₃⁻ (Kₐ₂ = 4.7 × 10⁻¹¹) and HCO₃⁻ + H⁺ ⇌ H₂CO₃ (Kₐ₁ = 4.3 × 10⁻⁷). The overall solubility at a given [H⁺] is obtained by solving the coupled mass‑balance and charge‑balance equations, often simplified by assuming that the dominant carbonate species is HCO₃⁻ at pH ≈ 8.3. Complexation can dramatically increase solubility by sequestering the metal ion. Silver chloride dissolves in aqueous ammonia because Ag⁺ forms the diamminesilver(I) complex: Ag⁺ + 2 NH₃ ⇌ [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺ with formation constant β₂ = 1.6 × 10⁷. The overall dissolution reaction AgCl(s) + 2 NH₃ ⇌ [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺ + Cl⁻ has an equilibrium constant K = Ksp β₂ ≈ 2.8 × 10⁻³, allowing appreciable AgCl dissolution at modest ammonia concentrations. In qualitative analysis, these principles are combined: group‑I cations are precipitated as chlorides by adding HCl (common‑ion effect), group‑II sulfides are precipitated by adjusting pH with H₂S in acidic medium (pH‑dependent solubility), and group‑III hydroxides are precipitated by raising pH with NH₄OH (common‑ion and pH effects together). Mastery of coupled equilibria is essential for predicting whether a precipitate will form under given solution conditions.

  • Assuming Henry’s constant is temperature‑independent when calculating gas solubility at different temperatures.
  • Using the pure‑solvent cryoscopic constant for a mixed‑solvent system without correcting for composition‑dependent Kf.
  • Neglecting activity coefficients in non‑ideal binary mixtures and applying Raoult’s law directly to predict azeotropic points.
  • Treating the common‑ion effect as a simple linear reduction of solubility without checking whether the added ion concentration truly dominates the equilibrium.
  • Ignoring the protonation equilibria of basic anions when evaluating pH‑dependent solubility of carbonates, sulfides, or phosphates.
  • Overlooking complex formation constants when a ligand (NH₃, CN⁻, EDTA) is present, leading to large underestimates of metal‑salt solubility.
  • Confusing the van’t Hoff factor i for strong electrolytes with the degree of dissociation for weak electrolytes in colligative‑property calculations.

These advanced considerations bridge textbook definitions and the quantitative problem‑solving required in competitive examinations.

hand/birational-geometry.html:
Log Minimal Model Program for Pairs and the Role of Discrepancies

The classical Minimal Model Program extends naturally to pairs (X, Δ) where Δ is an effective ℚ‑divisor with coefficients in [0,1]. The objective is to produce a log minimal model (Xₘ, Δₘ) such that KXₘ+Δₘ is nef. The steps mirror the absolute MMP: run a (K_X+Δ)‑negative extremal ray contraction, and when the contraction is small perform a log flip. The existence of log flips in all dimensions was settled by Birkar–Cascini–Hacon–McKernan (2010) using the theory of log canonical thresholds and the ACC conjecture for log canonical thresholds, later proved by Hacon–McKernan–Xu (2014). Discrepancies control the singularities of the pair: for a resolution f: Y → X write K_Y+Δ_Y = f^*(K_X+Δ) + Σ a_i E_i. The pair is terminal if all a_i > 0, canonical if a_i ≥ 0, klt if a_i > -1, and lc if a_i ≥ -1. These thresholds are stable under log flips, which guarantees that the category of klt (or lc) pairs is closed under the MMP. A crucial technical tool is the Negativity Lemma: if D is an f‑nef ℚ‑divisor with f_*D = 0 then D ≤ 0. This lemma underpins the comparison of discrepancies on two birational models and is used repeatedly in the proof of the Basepoint‑Free Theorem for pairs.

In practice, the log MMP reduces the classification of varieties with boundary to three building blocks: log Fano pairs (-(K_X+Δ) ample), log Calabi–Yau pairs (K_X+Δ ≡ 0), and pairs of log general type (K_X+Δ big). The Abundance Conjecture for pairs predicts that if K_X+Δ is nef then it is semi‑ample. This is known for surfaces, for threefolds (Kawamata, 1992), and for pairs with κ = 0 (Kawamata, 1998). The log version of the Cone Theorem states that the Mori cone NE(X) decomposes as NEK_X+Δ ≥ 0 + Σ ℝ₊[C_i] where each extremal ray ℝ₊[C_i] satisfies -(K_X+Δ)·C_i ≤ dim X + 1. This bound is sharp and is used to control the length of extremal rays in the log setting.

Termination of Flips and the Ascending Chain Condition

Termination of the MMP means that any sequence of log flips and divisorial contractions must be finite. For threefolds, Mori (1988) proved termination by a delicate analysis of the Hilbert scheme of curves and the boundedness of the length of extremal rays. In higher dimensions the problem splits into two parts: termination of flips for varieties of general type, and termination for all klt pairs. The breakthrough came with the proof of the ACC for log canonical thresholds (Hacon–McKernan–Xu, 2014). The ACC states that in a fixed dimension the set of log canonical thresholds lct(X, Δ; D) satisfies the ascending chain condition — there is no infinite strictly increasing sequence. This finiteness property forces the discrepancies that appear during a flip sequence to stabilize, which in turn forces the flip sequence to terminate. The proof uses the Minimal Model Program for pairs itself, together with the Boundedness of Complements (Birkar, 2016) which provides a uniform bound on the index of complements for klt pairs of bounded volume. As a corollary, the MMP terminates for all klt pairs in any dimension, assuming the existence of good minimal models for varieties of general type (proved by Birkar–Cascini–Hacon–McKernan, 2010). The termination theorem is the engine that makes the MMP an algorithm: one can start with any klt pair and after finitely many steps reach either a minimal model or a Mori fibre space.

Worked Example: Computing a Log Flip on a Toric Threefold
Consider the toric threefold X defined by the fan with rays v₁=(1,0,0), v₂=(0,1,0), v₃=(0,0,1), v₄=(-1,-1,-1) and the divisor Δ = ½ D₄ where D₄ corresponds to v₄. The pair (X, Δ) is klt. The ray generated by v₄ gives a (K_X+Δ)-negative extremal contraction φ: X → Z which is small (the exceptional locus is a curve). Describe the log flip X ⇢ X⁺.
The contraction φ contracts the invariant curve C corresponding to the cone ⟨v₁,v₂,v₃⟩. On the affine chart U = Spec ℂ[x,y,z] with torus action weights (1,1,1) the divisor Δ restricts to ½·{x=y=z=0}. The flip is obtained by replacing the cone ⟨v₁,v₂,v₃⟩ with the two cones ⟨v₁,v₂,v₄⟩ and ⟨v₁,v₃,v₄⟩ (or the symmetric choice). The resulting toric variety X⁺ has fan rays v₁,v₂,v₃,v₄ and the new maximal cones ⟨v₁,v₂,v₄⟩, ⟨v₁,v₃,v₄⟩, ⟨v₂,v₃,v₄⟩. The proper transform Δ⁺ of Δ is again ½ times the divisor corresponding to v₄. One checks that KX⁺+Δ⁺ is φ⁺-ample, so the birational map X ⇢ X⁺ is the required log flip. The discrepancies remain > -1, confirming the pair stays klt.
Exam Strategy: Recognising When a Flip Is Needed
In a problem asking to run the MMP on a given pair, first compute the intersection numbers (K_X+Δ)·C for all extremal curves C. If some intersection is negative and the corresponding contraction is small (exceptional locus codimension ≥ 2), a flip is mandatory. Remember that a divisorial contraction reduces the Picard number, while a flip preserves it. Keep track of the discrepancy condition: the flip exists only inside the klt (or lc) category. If the pair is only lc, you may need to pass to a dlt model before flipping.

Adjunction, Inversion of Adjunction, and the Canonical Bundle Formula

Adjunction relates the canonical divisor of a subvariety to that of the ambient space. For a normal variety X and a prime divisor S ⊂ X not contained in the support of Δ, the adjunction formula reads (K_X+Δ+S)|_S = K_S+Δ_S where Δ_S is the different, defined by the coefficients of the divisorial components of Δ|_S together with the contributions from the singularities of X along S. The Inversion of Adjunction (Kawamata, 1997; Kollár, 1997) states that (X, Δ+S) is plt (purely log terminal) near S if and only if (S, Δ_S) is klt. This equivalence is a cornerstone of the log MMP because it allows one to reduce questions about singularities of a pair to questions about a lower‑dimensional pair. The Canonical Bundle Formula (Kawamata, 1998; Ambro, 2005) generalises adjunction to a fibration f: X → Z with general fibre F a Calabi–Yau variety (K_F ≡ 0). It expresses K_X+Δ ∼_ℚ f^*(K_Z+Δ_Z+M_Z) where Δ_Z is the discriminant divisor encoding the singular fibres and M_Z is the moduli part, a nef ℚ‑divisor reflecting the variation of the fibres. The formula is essential for the Iitaka Conjecture and for the construction of minimal models for varieties with κ = 0. In the log setting, the formula holds for lc-trivial fibrations (Ambro, 2005) and the moduli part M_Z is known to be semi‑ample under the Abundance Conjecture for the base.

Applications include the proof that the moduli space of canonically polarised varieties is of general type (Kovács, 2000) and the construction of good minimal models for elliptic Calabi–Yau threefolds. The discriminant divisor Δ_Z is computed by the Kawamata–Viehweg vanishing theorem and the positivity of direct images (Kollár, 1986). The moduli part M_Z is often identified with the Hodge bundle on the base of the fibration, linking birational geometry to Hodge theory.

Boundedness of Varieties of General Type and Moduli of Canonical Models

While Birkar’s boundedness theorem (2018) covers Fano varieties, the analogous statement for varieties of general type is the boundedness of canonical models. A canonical model is a projective variety X with klt singularities and ample canonical divisor K_X. The theorem of Hacon–McKernan–Xu (2014) proves that for fixed dimension n and fixed volume V = (K_X)^n, the set of canonical models is bounded — they form a finite number of algebraic families. The proof uses the MMP for pairs to reduce to the case of a minimal model, then applies the ACC for log canonical thresholds to control the coefficients of the boundary, and finally invokes the Borisov–Alexeev boundedness for log canonical pairs of general type. A key technical ingredient is the Effective Basepoint‑Free Theorem (Hacon–McKernan, 2006) which gives an explicit multiple m such that |mK_X| is basepoint‑free depending only on n and V. This effectivity yields a uniform embedding of all such X into a fixed projective space, establishing boundedness.

The boundedness result underpins the construction of the moduli stack of canonically polarised varieties (Kollár–Shepherd‑Barron, 1988; Alexeev, 1996). The stack is proper and separated, and its coarse moduli space is a projective variety. Recent work (Liu–Xu–Zhuang, 2020) shows that the moduli space admits a good moduli space in the sense of Alper, and that K‑stability coincides with the existence of a Kähler‑Einstein metric on the canonical model (by the work of Berman–Boucksom–Jonsson, 2021). This ties the birational classification to differential geometry and provides a complete picture for varieties of general type analogous to the Fano case.

K‑Stability, Moduli of Fano Varieties, and the Yau‑Tian‑Donaldson Conjecture

K‑stability is an algebro‑geometric notion introduced by Tian (1997) and Donaldson (2002) to characterise the existence of Kähler‑Einstein metrics on Fano manifolds. A Fano variety X is K‑stable if for every normal test configuration (𝒳, ℒ) → 𝔸¹ with central fibre X₀, the Donaldson‑Futaki invariant DF(𝒳, ℒ) > 0 unless the test configuration is a product. The Yau‑Tian‑Donaldson conjecture (proved for smooth Fano manifolds by Chen–Donaldson–Sun, 2015) asserts that a Fano manifold admits a Kähler‑Einstein metric if and only if it is K‑stable. In the singular setting, the conjecture was extended by Odaka (2013) and proved by Xu–Zhuang (2020) for ℚ‑Fano varieties with klt singularities: K‑polystability is equivalent to the existence of a Kähler‑Einstein metric. The moduli space of K‑polystable Fano varieties (the K‑moduli space) was constructed by Jiang (2020) and by Blum–Xu (2021) using the theory of K‑stability thresholds and the boundedness of Fano varieties (Birkar, 2018). This moduli space is a proper Artin stack with a good moduli space which is a projective variety.

The interaction between the MMP and K‑stability is deep: a K‑polystable Fano variety is a log terminal model of itself, and the MMP provides a canonical way to degenerate any Fano variety to a K‑polystable one (the K‑semistable replacement). The delta invariant δ(X) = inf_E A_X(E)/S_X(E) (where A_X is the log discrepancy and S_X the expected vanishing order) gives a numerical criterion: X is K‑stable iff δ(X) > 1. This invariant is computable on toric Fano varieties via the moment polytope, linking combinatorics to stability. The boundedness of Fano varieties ensures that the set of possible delta invariants in a fixed dimension satisfies the ACC, a result proved by Blum–Liu–Xu (2022). These developments place the classification of Fano varieties on the same rigorous footing as the classification of varieties of general type.

  • Confusing the discrepancy thresholds: terminal > 0, canonical ≥ 0, klt > -1, lc ≥ -1; the strictness matters for flip existence.
  • Assuming every extremal contraction is divisorial; small contractions require flips, and the flip may not exist outside the klt category.
  • Neglecting the role of the different in adjunction; the boundary on the divisor is not simply the restriction of Δ.
  • Treating the ACC for log canonical thresholds as a black box without knowing it is equivalent to termination of flips.
  • Overlooking that boundedness of Fano varieties requires klt singularities and a fixed volume; smoothness alone is not enough in high dimension.
  • Mixing up K‑stability with slope stability; the Donaldson‑Futaki invariant is the correct numerical test for Fano varieties.
  • Forgetting that the canonical bundle formula produces a moduli part which is only known to be nef, not necessarily semi‑ample, without abundance.

hand/chromatic-homotopy.html:
The Thick Subcategory Theorem and Classification of Localizing Subcategories

The thick subcategory theorem, proved by Hopkins and Smith in 1998, gives a complete classification of the thick subcategories of the category of finite spectra. A thick subcategory is a full triangulated subcategory closed under retracts. The theorem states that for each integer n ≥ 0 the collection C_n of finite spectra of type ≥ n forms a thick subcategory, and every non‑zero thick subcategory of finite spectra equals C_n for a unique n. Here a finite spectrum X has type n if K(m)_*(X) = 0 for m < n and K(n)_*(X) ≠ 0, where K(m) denotes the m‑th Morava K‑theory at a fixed prime p. The proof uses the nilpotence theorem to show that any map between finite spectra which is zero on all Morava K‑theories is nilpotent, and then applies the periodicity theorem to produce v_n self‑maps on type‑n spectra. The classification has immediate consequences: the Bousfield lattice of the stable homotopy category restricted to finite spectra is a chain 0 = ⟨K(∞)⟩ < ⟨K(n)⟩ < … < ⟨K(0)⟩ = ⟨S⁰⟩, and any smashing localization on finite spectra is given by smashing with a telescope T(n) of a v_n self‑map. The theorem also extends to the classification of localizing subcategories of the K(n)‑local category via the work of Hovey and Strickland, where the only localizing subcategories are 0 and the whole category.

Gross–Hopkins Duality and Brown–Comenetz Duality in Chromatic Homotopy

Gross–Hopkins duality identifies the Spanier–Whitehead dual of the Morava E‑theory spectrum E_n up to a suspension. Concretely, let I_n denote the Brown–Comenetz dual of the K(n)‑local sphere; then there is an equivalence I_n ≃ Σn²−n E_n^∨, where E_n^∨ is the functional dual of E_n in the K(n)‑local category. The duality is a consequence of the fact that the Morava stabilizer group G_n acts on E_n with a fundamental class in degree n²−n, and the continuous cohomology of G_n with coefficients in E_n_* satisfies a Poincaré duality of dimension n²−n. The Brown–Comenetz dual of K(n) itself is Σ2(p^n−1)n K(n), a formula first proved by Gross and Hopkins using the theory of Lubin–Tate formal groups and the determinant of the adjoint representation of G_n. This duality has several applications: it yields a concrete description of the Picard group of the K(n)‑local category, it implies that the K(n)‑local sphere is a dualizable object with dual given by a shift of itself, and it provides the input for the chromatic fracture square that relates LK(n)X to LE(n)X and LE(n−1)X. Moreover, the duality is compatible with the action of the extended Morava stabilizer group, giving a G_n‑equivariant equivalence after passing to homotopy fixed points.

Worked Example: Computing the Brown–Comenetz Dual of K(1) at p = 2
Let p = 2 and n = 1. The Morava K‑theory K(1) has coefficient ring K(1)_* = 𝔽₂[v₁, v₁-1] with |v₁| = 2. Using the Gross–Hopkins formula, the Brown–Comenetz dual IK(1) is Σ2(p1−1)·1 K(1) = Σ2 K(1). Verify this by computing the Anderson dual of the K(1)‑local sphere and comparing with the known Picard group PicK(1) ≅ ℤ/2 × ℤ₂.
The Gross–Hopkins duality theorem states that the Brown–Comenetz dual of K(n) is Σ2(p^n−1)n K(n). For n = 1, p = 2 we have 2(p1−1)·1 = 2·1·1 = 2. Hence IK(1) ≃ Σ² K(1). The K(1)‑local sphere S⁰K(1) is self‑dual up to a shift of 2, which matches the known generator of the Picard group: the class of Σ² S⁰K(1) corresponds to the non‑trivial element in the ℤ/2 factor. The ℤ₂ factor comes from the determinant of the G₁‑action on the Lubin–Tate deformation space. Thus the computation is consistent with the full Picard group description.
Exam Strategy: Recognising Duality Shifts
When a question asks for the Brown–Comenetz dual of K(n) or the Gross–Hopkins dual of E_n, write down the exponent formula immediately: 2(p^n−1)n for K(n) and n²−n for E_n. Do not attempt to re‑derive the Poincaré duality dimension during the exam; memorise the two numbers and the fact that the dual of the K(n)‑local sphere is a shift of itself. This saves time and avoids sign errors.

The Adams–Novikov Spectral Sequence and Chromatic Filtration

The Adams–Novikov spectral sequence (ANSS) is the primary computational tool for the stable homotopy groups of spheres. Its E₂‑term is the continuous cohomology of the moduli stack MFG of formal groups with coefficients in the quasi‑coherent sheaf ω⊗t associated to the grading. The chromatic filtration on MFG by height of formal groups induces a filtration on the ANSS: the E₂‑page splits into layers E₂s,t(n) corresponding to height n formal groups. The monochromatic layer at height n is precisely the continuous cohomology of the Morava stabilizer group G_n with coefficients in E_n_*, which computes the K(n)‑local homotopy groups via the homotopy fixed point spectral sequence E₂s,t = H^s_c(G_n; E_n_t) ⇒ πt−s LK(n) S⁰. The chromatic spectral sequence (CSS) assembles these layers: its E₁‑term is the direct sum over n of the homotopy groups of the monochromatic fibers M_n = fib(LE(n) → LE(n−1)), and it converges to the homotopy groups of the K(n)‑localization of a finite spectrum. The interaction between the ANSS and the CSS is governed by the chromatic convergence theorem, which guarantees that for a finite spectrum X the natural map X → holim_n L_n X is an equivalence. In practice, computations up to the 61‑stem (as of 2015) use a combination of the ANSS at heights 1 and 2, the tmf‑based spectral sequence at height 2, and the known periodic families (α, β, γ) detected by v₁ and v₂ self‑maps.

The X(n)-Construction and the Proof of the Nilpotence Theorem

The nilpotence theorem of Devinatz, Hopkins, and Smith (1988) asserts that a map f : X → Y of finite spectra is nilpotent if and only if MU_*(f) = 0. The proof constructs a tower of spectra X(n) for each n ≥ 0, called the X(n)‑construction, with the property that MU ∧ X(n) ≃ ⋁i Σk_i MU and that the map X → holim_n X(n) is an equivalence. Each X(n) is built by iteratively killing the ideal (p, v₁, …, vn−1) in MU_* using cofiber sequences, and the resulting spectrum has the same MU‑homology as a wedge of suspensions of MU. The key step is to show that the map MU → X(n) induces an isomorphism on MU_* after inverting v_n, which follows from the Landweber exact functor theorem applied to the formal group law of height n. The nilpotence theorem then follows by observing that if MU_*(f) = 0, then f becomes zero after smashing with X(n) for all n, and the homotopy limit argument forces f to be nilpotent. The X(n) spectra also provide the input for the periodicity theorem: the existence of v_n self‑maps on type‑n finite spectra is deduced by analyzing the action of the Morava stabilizer group on the homotopy groups of X(n). This construction is the geometric heart of chromatic homotopy theory, linking the algebraic structure of MU_* to the geometric classification of finite spectra.

Smith–Toda Complexes, Type‑n Spectra, and the Periodicity Theorem

For each n ≥ 0 there exists a finite spectrum V(n) of type n, known as a Smith–Toda complex, constructed by iteratively attaching cells to kill the lower height Morava K‑theories. The original construction by Smith and Toda (1970s) produced V(0) = S⁰, V(1) = the mod‑p Moore spectrum, and V(2) as a 2‑cell complex with cells in dimensions 0 and 2p−2. For higher n the existence of V(n) was proved by Ravenel using the nilpotence theorem and the periodicity theorem. The periodicity theorem states that any finite spectrum X of type n admits a v_n self‑map v : Σd X → X for some d > 0, unique up to a unit in the coefficient ring K(n)_*. The telescope T(n) = colim (X → Σ-d X → Σ-2d X → …) is then a K(n)‑local spectrum whose homotopy groups are the v_n‑periodic homotopy groups of X. The thick subcategory theorem implies that the Bousfield class of T(n) depends only on n, not on the choice of X or v. The failure of the telescope conjecture shows that the localization L_n^f at the wedge K(0) ∨ … ∨ K(n) is not equivalent to smashing with T(n) in general; however, for finite spectra the two localizations agree after K(n)‑localization. The Smith–Toda complexes also play a central role in the computation of the homotopy groups of spheres via the chromatic spectral sequence, because the monochromatic layer M_n is built from the fibers of the maps LE(n) V(n) → LE(n−1) V(n).

  • Confusing the height of a formal group with the chromatic level of a localization; height n corresponds to K(n) but the localization L_n uses the wedge K(0) ∨ … ∨ K(n).
  • Assuming the telescope conjecture holds for all n; it is false for n ≥ 2 at large primes and remains open only for n = 1.
  • Misapplying the Gross–Hopkins duality shift: the dual of K(n) is Σ2(p^n−1)n K(n), while the dual of E_n is Σn²−n E_n^∨.
  • Thinking the thick subcategory theorem classifies all localizing subcategories of the stable homotopy category; it only classifies thick subcategories of finite spectra.
  • Neglecting the role of the Morava stabilizer group G_n in the homotopy fixed point spectral sequence; the continuous cohomology H^*_c(G_n; E_n_*) is the E₂‑term for K(n)‑local homotopy.
  • Believing that the Adams–Novikov spectral sequence collapses at E₂ for finite spectra; it has many non‑trivial differentials, especially at heights 1 and 2.
  • Overlooking the distinction between the X(n) construction (used to prove nilpotence) and the Smith–Toda complexes V(n) (used to realise type‑n spectra).
The advanced sections above complete the chromatic homotopy overview with precise theorems, computational tools, and the key counterexamples that shape current research.
